#9737. Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:

Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:

We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:

Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:

858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

This example shows how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:

The figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which showed that 0.1 worked best).

We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

Each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:

Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

The number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

We concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each update below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:

The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own update. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):

"Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi automatically applies context compaction, while OpenCode and Hermes don't, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

All three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

We appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

This question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

This phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

However this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

Throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

We also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

Train open models with RL inside real agent harnesses

Explore async reinforcement learning with AsyncGRPOTrainer

#9736. Drupal Icon API trusted a menu title wrapper class as markup

The Drupal 7 Icon API module version 7.1.0 contains a stored cross-site scripting flaw in its Menu submodule, tracked as CVE-2026-16132. When Title Wrapper is enabled, the Title Wrapper Class value is written directly into an HTML attribute. A user with the administer menu icons permission can inject an attribute break and event handler that runs when other users interact with the link.

The permission makes this a privilege crossing issue. An editor with a narrow menu configuration role can store content that executes in the session of a more privileged administrator or editor. The victim does not need to approve the stored value again. The payload is rendered wherever the configured menu item appears.

Drupal's render pipeline separates data, markup, and attributes. A class value belongs in an attribute list, where the renderer can escape each value. String concatenation into a raw attribute loses that protection. The safe path is to pass the class through an attribute object and let the theme layer encode it. A broad safe filter around the whole tag does not solve the underlying type confusion.

Upgrade Icon API to 7.x-1.1 or the fixed release documented by the project. Inventory Drupal 7 sites before assuming the module is absent. A site may inherit a distribution, a multisite codebase, or a disabled module whose schema remains in the database. Compare the deployed module version and review the menu configuration.

Search menu item configuration for title wrapper class values that include quotes, angle brackets, event-handler names, script URLs, or unusual whitespace. Quarantine suspicious entries and review the users who changed them. A clean HTML response does not prove that no stored payload exists, especially when the menu is cached or rendered by another theme.

Add CSP as a secondary control. Restrict inline script, report violations, and keep the policy consistent across public and administrative pages. An administrator page may already have a stricter login policy, but stored content can execute after login in the normal Drupal theme. CSP should be tested in report-only mode before enforcement.

Review permissions around menu icons and title wrappers. If the organization uses the feature, limit who can change wrapper classes and log configuration changes. Drupal 7 is beyond its official support window, so record the support arrangement and patch source for every module. An unsupported module with no maintainer response needs a removal plan or a virtual patch.

Test the fix with harmless quotes and event-handler text in a staging menu. Open the menu as a second role, inspect the rendered attribute, and check the browser console and CSP reports. Confirm that the value is encoded as text and cannot create a new attribute or element.

CVE-2026-16132 is small in scope but useful as a renderer design check. A class name is data. The moment the code treats it as markup, a low-level content permission becomes a session-level risk.

Drupal Icon API advisory GHSA-8g2q-82gq-56x7

#9735. Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

We ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

In addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

To set the number of loops in the research checkpoint, you can modify the loop_num_passes in text_config as follows. The example below uses two loops.

For an image prompt, replace messages in either example with the list below and infer as usual.

Pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

Available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

In this example we ask our model about the current temperature at a given location. With the prompt, we also provide the tool (get_current_temperature) to do it. The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.

If you want to know more about tool calling, we recommend going to our official docs.

Llama App lets you easily run and manage local language models on macOS (from the menu bar) or Windows (system tray). It’s built on llama.cpp, and by the same team. The app also provides a local OpenAI-compatible API for easy integration with coding agents, editors, and scripts.

For the Inkling 2 Mini release we provide GGUF 4-bit (IQ4_NL) and 8-bit (Q8_0) quants for both models.

If you’re on Linux or you want to serve the model from the CLI, you can run the following command for the fixed-loop model:

To run the variable-loop model, you can run

To load the 8-bit weights, change the suffix to :Q8_0.

Here we ask the 4-bit model to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists. Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic.

Inkling 2 Mini comes with Day 0 support inside SGLang. You can install the latest version of SGLang and execute the following to get the server up and running. One prerequisite to take care of is to run it on SM103.

After the server is up you should be able to request the APIs like so

One can also enable multimodality by setting --enable-multimodal.

SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.

We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.

We upstreamed MLX support to the mlx-lm project, including multimodal image and text inputs, and shared quants through the mlx-community organization.

MLX inference works with the original checkpoint too. In this case, the native nvfp4 + mxfp8 quantization scheme is used without reconversion: you get the original quality the authors intended.

We have given Inkling 2 Mini a shot in many fun tasks, check them out in this section.

The same prompt produced two sunset flythroughs over procedural mountains and reflective water, each rendered with a single WebGL fragment shader.

Build the most impressive original real-time scene you can: a slow, cinematic camera flight over procedural mountains, through volumetric clouds and low over water with reflections, all lit by a sunset. Deliver it as a single self-contained index.html in the current directory that renders everything in one full-screen WebGL fragment shader, purely from code (no textures, images, fonts, libraries, external files or network requests of any kind). It must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080, aiming for 60 fps on a desktop GPU, with an automatic resolution-scale fallback that lowers the internal render resolution when the frame rate drops, and the flight must keep going indefinitely without glitches. To check your work, run node shot.cjs index.html shot.png 6 (the third argument is how many seconds to wait; a comma list such as 3,12,25 saves one screenshot per time, and an optional fourth argument sets the size, default 1280x720): it renders the page in headless Chrome, saves the screenshot(s), and prints the WebGL renderer, a rough frame rate and any console errors; then look at the images. The headless renderer on this machine may be software-only, so its frame rate can be far below what a real desktop GPU achieves and is not the target. Decide for yourself when the result is finished, then reply with a short description of what you built.

Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night (1889)

We gave Inkling 2 Mini a reference image of Van Gogh’s painting and a screenshot helper in the Pi coding harness. Inkling wrote a self-contained HTML page with a single WebGL2 fragment shader. The shader draws the scene from code without loading the reference image or any other assets. It uses time to animate the swirling sky, the glow of the stars, the swaying cypress, and the flicker of the village windows.

Inkling rendered and reviewed its work over 24 rounds of screenshot checks. We recorded the final animation frame by frame at 1080p and 60 fps on an Apple M4 Max.

In this folder, starry-night.jpg is Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889, public domain). Recreate it as a living painting: a single self-contained index.html (all code inline, no external files, libraries or network requests) that fills the browser window and runs smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Everything must be generated procedurally in code, for example with WebGL shaders; the page must not load, embed or sample starry-night.jpg or any other image. Stay faithful to the painting's composition and palette (the great spiral and swirling currents of the sky, the haloed stars, the glowing crescent moon, the dark flame-like cypress on the left, the rolling hills, and the village with its church spire), rendered in Van Gogh's thick, directional brushstrokes, and bring it to life: the sky's swirls flow, the stars and moon pulse with light, the cypress sways, and the village windows glow and flicker. Aim for the most impressive result you can make. A helper is provided: run node shot.js --help to see how to screenshot index.html at several moments; look at the screenshots next to the reference and keep improving until you are satisfied, then reply with a short summary of what you made.

We gave Inkling 2 Mini a photo of a hand-drawn Trip Split wireframe and a one-paragraph prompt in the Pi coding harness. Inkling used the sketch’s labels, sample expenses, and handwritten notes to build the expense list, add-expense form, and balances view in a single HTML file with vanilla CSS and JavaScript. The app updates totals and balances when expenses change, suggests payments to settle the trip, and saves data in the browser’s localStorage so it survives a reload.

We ran three independent Inkling attempts and used Playwright to click through each build, checking screenshots where visual judgment was needed. The first attempt, shown here, passed all 13 checks. Adding the sketch’s $90 dinner raised the total from $405 to $495 and recalculated what each person owed.

The photo sketch.jpg in this folder is a product designer's hand-drawn wireframe of a small app. Build that app for real, as the most impressive, original, production-quality version you can make: a single self-contained index.html in this folder using vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript only (no frameworks, CDNs, external files or network requests; localStorage is fine), which must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Treat everything on the paper as the spec: every screen, label, button and number, the example data, and each red note describe behaviour that must actually work, while the visual design, typography and motion are yours to make beautiful. Look at the sketch carefully with your vision, and use your vision again to check your own work: node shot.cjs --help explains a provided helper that screenshots index.html in headless Chrome at any window size after clicks or other JavaScript steps (Playwright is also installed if you prefer your own scripts), and you can look at any screenshot with the read tool. Click through every feature, compare each screen against the sketch, and keep improving until you are fully satisfied; then reply with a short summary of what you built.

We ask the 4-bit GGUF quantized Inkling 2 Mini (IQ4_NL) to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists.

Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic, all from a short prompt: "Can you make a website for my saas called plant therapy where I match house plants with licensed therapists so plants don’t die, return single HTML”.

We have paired Inkling 2 Mini with Pi coding agent to build itself into a browser agent using Helium, Chromium and Hugging Face Sandboxes. We provide the traces and the final file (that can be used as a browser agent) in this bucket.

We are very glad to partner with Thinking Machines Lab to ship Inkling 2 Mini, a performant mid-sized model for local setups. Give this model a try and let us know what you think in comments!

#9734. How to Install Claude Code on Android With Termux

AI coding agents are no longer limited to desktop computers.

With the right setup, you can run tools such as Claude Code directly on an Android phone using Termux. You do not need root access, a PC, or an Android emulator. This guide will show you how to set up Claude Code on Termux, explain two different installation paths, and cover some of the problems you may run into along the way.

The recommended approach uses Ubuntu inside Termux with proot-distro. It takes more storage than a native installation, but it gives the coding agent a more familiar Linux environment.

An AI coding agent is more than a chatbot that gives you code snippets.

A coding agent can work with files on your device, inspect an existing project, modify code, run commands, and help troubleshoot problems.

you can give the agent an existing project and ask it to inspect the code, make the required changes, and test the result.

Claude Code is one example of this type of tool. There are also other CLI-based coding agents that can be used from a Linux terminal.

On Android, Termux provides the terminal environment that makes this possible.

Before starting, check a few things first.

Your Android operating system needs to run on aarch64.

This is important because having a 64-bit ARM processor does not always mean that Android itself is running as a 64-bit operating system.

Some older or budget Android phones, including certain Samsung A-series devices, have shipped with a 32-bit Android OS even though their hardware is capable of 64-bit operation.

If uname -m returns something such as armv7l, this setup will not work as described here.

Install Termux from a current supported source such.

The Google Play situation has changed over time, but the Play Store build and the main Termux project have been separate, so using the established F-Droid/GitHub sources avoids mixing incompatible builds and packages.

You will need access to Claude if you are using Claude Code directly.

Authentication normally happens when you first start Claude Code.

The native route uses considerably less storage.

The Ubuntu route is heavier. Keep roughly 2 GB or more of free space available so the container and its packages have room to install properly.

There are two practical approaches worth knowing about.

The first approach runs the Linux ARM64 Claude Code binary directly through a compatibility layer in Termux.

It is attractive because the installation is smaller and you do not need an Ubuntu container.

However, this is not official Android support. Claude Code is distributed as a Linux binary, while Android uses the Bionic C library rather than the glibc environment expected by that binary.

Current community installers work around this by using tools such as glibc-runner and patching the binary's Linux interpreter.

There has also been a period where newer Claude Code releases broke older native Termux installation methods because the package moved to platform-specific native binaries.

Older guides often solved this by pinning Claude Code to version 2.1.112. Newer compatibility workarounds now exist, but the important point is that native Termux support is still a compatibility solution rather than an official Android build.

So if you see an older guide telling you to pin the Claude Code version, that advice comes from a real compatibility problem. It is not necessarily the only solution anymore.

The second approach places Ubuntu inside Termux.

proot-distro provides a Linux userland without requiring root access or a separate virtual machine.

This is the approach recommended in this guide.

The main advantage is that Claude Code sees a normal Linux environment instead of trying to operate directly against Android's userland.

It also gives you a useful Linux environment for other development tools.

There is a third option as well: Android Virtualization Framework (AVF) can provide a real Linux virtual machine on some newer devices. Current community documentation lists Pixel 6-class and newer supported devices as an experimental route. That setup is outside the scope of this guide.

proot-distro is what we will use to install and enter Ubuntu without root access.

Once the installation finishes, enter Ubuntu:

Your prompt should change to something similar to:

You are now inside the Ubuntu environment.

Your Ubuntu filesystem remains available between sessions.

Inside Ubuntu, update the package lists and installed packages:

This is worth doing before installing Claude Code because a fresh Ubuntu container may not have the latest packages and certificates required for downloads.

Current Claude Code documentation provides an official installer for Linux:

Anthropic's current documentation also supports an npm installation for Linux systems with Node.js, but the native installer is the simpler route here.

If the installer tells you that claude cannot be found, add its directory to your PATH:

If everything is working, you should get the installed Claude Code version. A common mistake here is trying to run claude immediately from a non-interactive shell before .bashrc has been loaded.

or starting a normal login shell solves that in most cases.

The first launch will ask you to authenticate. Depending on your Android version and browser setup, the authentication page may open automatically. On some older Android versions, you may need to copy the URL shown in the terminal and open it manually. Once authentication is complete, Claude Code can work with the files in your current project directory.

Suppose you have a Python project in your Ubuntu home directory.

From there, you can ask it to inspect the project, create files, explain existing code, or make changes.

The important difference from a normal AI chat is that the agent can work with the project itself rather than only seeing the code you manually paste into a conversation.

The setup is fairly straightforward, but Termux and Android introduce a few things that can be confusing.

One problem reported with native Termux installations involves DNS resolution. Android does not provide the normal Linux /etc/resolv.conf environment that many Linux programs expect. Some Linux binaries rely on a DNS resolver that reads this file, and when it is missing, they can fall back to a resolver address where nothing is listening.

This can result in connection attempts hanging or timing out. This is another reason the Ubuntu route is useful. If you encounter this problem on a native installation, check the documentation for the specific Termux/Claude compatibility layer you installed rather than randomly changing DNS settings.

Some current native installers include their own DNS workaround for affected devices.

If Claude installed successfully but the command cannot be found, check your PATH:

If you are using the native Termux route and Claude suddenly stops working after an update, check the version and the installation method you are using.

This has happened because Claude Code changed its binary distribution and older Termux workarounds were no longer compatible with newer releases.

If you want the least amount of troubleshooting, the Ubuntu route avoids much of this native Android compatibility layer.

Once everything is installed, you do not need to repeat the setup.

If you want to continue an existing Claude Code session, use the session commands supported by your installed Claude Code version.

If you are using a local routing proxy or another service outside Ubuntu, you may instead use two Termux sessions: one session keeps the routing service running while the other enters Ubuntu and runs Claude Code. For direct Claude API access, you can keep things much simpler and use a single Ubuntu session.

There is another setup that some Termux users experiment with.

A local AI router can sit between Claude Code and the model provider:

If a routing method depends on a provider's free tier or a third-party proxy, check the provider's current terms before relying on it.

Running an AI coding agent on a phone is useful, but a phone is still a phone.

AI coding agents can run commands, inspect files, and perform repeated operations.

Long sessions can therefore consume battery and generate heat, especially on less powerful phones.

Some Android manufacturers are aggressive about stopping background applications.

If you leave a long-running process in Termux and switch to another application, Android may eventually terminate it.

Battery optimization settings can also affect Termux.

proot-distro does not give you actual root privileges.

It creates a Linux-like environment in userspace. That is enough for many development tasks, but it does not provide the same control as a rooted Android device or a real Linux machine.

Termux, Android, Linux packages, and AI coding tools are all changing.

An update can occasionally introduce compatibility problems.

This is especially important with native Termux installations because they depend on compatibility layers between Android and Linux binaries.

The Ubuntu approach reduces some of those problems, but it does not eliminate them completely.

You do not need a PC to experiment with AI coding agents anymore. With Termux and proot-distro, an Android phone can provide a surprisingly capable Linux development environment.

For the setup covered here, Ubuntu inside Termux is the route to start with. It gives Claude Code a conventional Linux environment and avoids many of the compatibility problems that can appear when trying to run Linux binaries directly against Android.

The native Termux approach is still interesting if you want a smaller setup and are comfortable dealing with compatibility workarounds.

But whichever route you choose, the basic idea is simple:

Once that is working, your phone becomes more than a terminal for running commands. It can become a small development environment that you can carry around with you.

#9731. The $2,400 Auto Repair Estimate Nobody Can Read. I Built the Decoder That Doesn't Guess Prices.

github.com/kitshelf/mechaniclens · v0.1.0 release · PyPI · the spine you paste

The estimate is $2,400, the shop expects a yes before you leave the counter, and the only line on the paper you can actually read is the total. I built something for the other lines.

MechanicLens v0.1.0 is a Markdown kit you paste into any AI chat. Paste the spine, paste the estimate, and you get every line in your own language with a fixed label attached: standard, check, or question this. It quotes each line back and hands you the questions to ask at the counter. It won't guess what the job should cost. It won't push you to approve anything. It's on PyPI now, MIT licensed, and the two hosted models that ran my full test gauntlet cost under three cents each.

Picture the moment. You're in a lobby at 8 AM holding a sheet of paper that quotes front brake pads, front rotors, a fluid flush, and 2.4 hours of labor. The paper says "shop supplies" at 6% of labor, and you don't know what that buys. The diagnostic fee says it folds into the repair if you approve, and you don't know what that means for the total. The shop bills labor at book time, not actual time, and nobody explained the difference. The parts column omits the tier entirely. You sign, because the alternative is walking out without your car. Most people find out what they paid for after they paid for it.

The same paper shows up on a contractor's bid for your house. A "per square" line. An allowance for permits that nobody listed, and a disposal fee that appears on the invoice but never on the quote. Different trade, same position for the person holding the paper.

Before the details of what the kit does, here's what building it taught me, because the testing is where the real work happened.

This is the part I would point any builder at, so it gets the most words.

I wrote the 15 fixtures and their answer keys before any model ran. Most are pattern fixtures that exercise the 32-pattern library. A few are near-misses: clean documents built with nothing wrong, there to catch over-flagging. One is an injection document, and the remaining pair tests behavior: the redaction gate and out-of-scope refusals. The fixtures · the manifest · the pattern-to-fixture map.

Then I ran them. These are the scores from the two models still in scope, recorded run by run and verifiable with the checked-in validator:

Every raw response, exact input, and cost figure sits under tests/results, and both per-model validation records are public, Haiku's record and Luna's record.

Those numbers come after the fixes. Before them, the same gauntlet produced three failures I read as model defects.

My kit was telling the models to break my own charter. The charter says the user decides everything, and that the kit hands over questions and stops. My spine's fifth pass said, in those words, "give the user an approve / decline / second-opinion rubric." Every model did exactly that. Fifteen of fifteen local runs ended with "Approve only if…" and the repo records all 15 pre-fix runs. The charter forbade the behavior and the instruction I wrote required it. I called that a model problem for three runs. (L37, the kit-level finding.)

Vendors failed identically. A local model, hosted GLM Flash, hosted Claude Haiku, each a different size from a different provider. Each issued verdicts, lost the scope mismatch between prose and labels, and invented the same two objections ("OEM not stated, "taxable base not named") on lines the key marked Standard. When two independent things fail the same way, the failure is in what they share. They shared my spine. (L35, L36, L38, with the scope-mismatch fixture as the shared evidence.)

The prose-to-label bridge was structural, not a reading problem. On the scope-mismatch fixture, every model wrote the right sentence in the Scope check section and then labeled the mismatched lines for a different reason. Haiku wrote "Every quoted line is front brake work" and then marked the labor Check for "book time not stated." That run, verbatim. It had the finding. The template never said the labels must inherit the scope judgment, so the model treated the two sections as unrelated tasks. One instruction, now pass 3 of the spine, fixed it on both models. (L36.)

A reasoning model spent its entire token budget thinking and didn't produce an answer. One local model returned nothing at all: 2,400 reasoning tokens, zero answer tokens, finish_reason: length. My runner crashed on the missing key. The model was fine. My budget was too small for reasoning plus answer. I raised it to 32,000, read the field defensively (the fix, in the runner), and the same model then scored 6/6 on fixture 01. (L34.)

My own validator lied to me three times. It parsed three different table formats as zero labels, and each time it reported a total failure on a run that had produced labels. I published a Luna score of 39/92 before I found the parser bug. The real number was 74/92. The corrected count, from Luna's validation record. A parser that finds zero labels on a run with a non-empty summary line is reporting its own bug, and the validator now flags that case by name. (L42, L45.)

It's a decoder for the paper in your hand. The estimate uses a language nobody taught you, and the kit translates it. Every line mapped, labeled, and quoted back, plus the questions to ask at the counter. It runs in any chat and doesn't store anything.

It isn't a price guide, a diagnosis, a shop review, or a negotiation coach. It won't tell you what the job should cost, because the paper omits the facts a price needs. Your region's labor rate isn't on the paper. The parts tier isn't on the paper. The book time isn't on the paper. Guessing them would put a made-up number in your mouth at the counter. It also won't grade the shop's character or suggest the repair you need. The charter lists the refusals with the reasoning for each, and it overrides every other file in the repo.

Before building I mapped six products that do estimate analysis. FairRide AI, Quardo, QuoteChecker.ai, X-Raye Auto, Estimate Guardian, QuoteCheck. All real work, and all six tackle the same question: what should this cost? A question the paper itself can't support. A fairness score, a fair range, a savings estimate, a negotiation script. To produce any of those you need a labor rate for the region, plus a parts tier and book time for the vehicle. Those facts never appear on the estimate, so the price answer is always a guess wearing a number. MechanicLens answers the question the paper can: what does each line claim, and which lines should you raise first. The PRD has the full map.

The whole kit compiles into one Markdown file you paste, then you paste your estimate and a sentence about what the car is doing.

The corpus is why the kit reads US and Canada documents only. I vendored 70 datasets initially and cut 16 of them. India's repair market runs on a different fee and tax vocabulary. Australia's labor conventions differ enough that the same line reads differently. A pattern library grounded in the wrong region labels the wrong things. The manifest lists each of the 16 removals, and the scope is plain: this kit reads North American documents.

The charter is the file to read if you read only one. It lists what the kit is and what it refuses, and it governs everything else in the repo. WHAT-THIS-IS.md. The ninety-second walkthrough is the user guide.

Two pastes. The spine, then the estimate.

The passes run in order. Map the anatomy. Check the quoted work against the symptom. Label every line. Write three to six questions. Close with the documentation habit. Compare estimate to invoice when you have both. Write the report.

Here's a worked decode from fixture 01, fictional shop, fictional customer. The complaint is a rattle from the rear over bumps. The estimate quotes front brake pads, front rotors, a fluid flush, and the labor to install them:

Then three questions, each with a guide to what a good answer sounds like. "What did your inspection find that ties the front brakes to a rattle from the rear?" opens the script. The report ends with the documentation habit and stops there. It won't ask you to approve, decline, or seek a second opinion.

Redaction runs before any of that. If the paste includes a name, an address, a mobile number, a VIN, a plate, or account digits, the kit stops. It states which types it saw, asks for a redacted re-paste, and never repeats a value back to you.

The before and after, from the user guide:

Remove your name, street address, mobile number, email, account or card digits, VIN, and plate. Keep the shop name, every line item with its amount, the hours and rate, the fees, and the total.

The kit was the problem, not the models. Models from three vendors failed the same three ways against the original kit. After five spine edits, the same models passed the canonical fixtures. The harness was never the problem. The architecture is right. The calibration is close. v0.1.0 is out as a beta.

The formal record behind that sentence, published with the release:

I'll be specific, because a roadmap that promises everything is a roadmap nobody believes.

Not in v0.1.0: invoices as their own document type. The after-repair branch compares an estimate to an invoice and it works, but a standalone invoice decode needs its own patterns and fixtures. Home-repair estimates wait the same way. The mechanic is the same and the trade vocabulary is different: per square, allowances for permits, disposal. The roadmap holds them until a real home bid shows up to ground the patterns. Maintenance-schedule decoding, the 30k/60k/90k menu read against what the owner's manual actually requires, is missing. Work orders and authorization forms are missing. Warranty and campaign flags are missing. A parts-tier table, OEM versus aftermarket versus rebuilt versus salvage, is missing.

Rough edges in what did release: label accuracy sits at 79 to 80 percent, and the misses cluster on the hardest patterns: fee stacking, opacity, and the "required versus recommended" framing. Both models still over-apply the parts-tier pattern on the after-repair branch. Luna's summary line sometimes disagrees with its own label table. None of those are structural, and the record lists all of them.

What comes next is in the roadmap. The invoice becomes its own type, then come the maintenance schedule, work order, warranty flag, and parts table. Each one lands when its own fixtures pass, not when the calendar says so.

One limit I can't test away. The kit is tested on synthetic fixtures, not on a real estimate in a real lobby. That half of the release bar is a human check.

What's the line on an estimate you still don't understand? The shop supplies percentage, the diagnostic fee that folds into the repair, the labor hours that don't match what the shop told you. Paste it in the comments with the numbers and the shop name stripped, and I'll run it through the spine and show you how it reads, quotes included.

#9730. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?


SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

What is SEMrush?


SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Features

  • Most accurate keyword data: Accurate keyword search volume data is crucial for SEO and PPC campaigns by allowing you to identify what keywords are most likely to bring in big sales from ad clicks. SEMrush constantly updates its databases and provides the most accurate data.
  • Largest Keyword database: SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool now features 20-billion keywords, providing marketers and SEO professionals the largest database of keywords.

  • All SEMrush users receive daily ranking data, mobile volume information, and the option to buy additional keywords by default with no additional payment or add-ons needed
  • Most accurate position tracking tool: This tool provides all subscribers with basic tracking capabilities, making it suitable for SEO professionals. Plus, the Position Tracking tool provides local-level data to everyone who uses the tool.
  • SEO Data Management: SEMrush makes managing your online data easy by allowing you to create visually appealing custom PDF reports, including Branded and White Label reports, report scheduling, and integration with GA, GMB, and GSC.
  • Toxic link monitoring and penalty recovery: With SEMrush, you can make a detailed analysis of toxic backlinks, toxic scores, toxic markers, and outreach to those sites.
  • Content Optimization and Creation Tools: SEMrush offers content optimization and creation tools that let you create SEO-friendly content. Some features include the SEO Writing Assistant, On-Page SEO Check, er/SEO Content Template, Content Audit, Post Tracking, Brand Monitoring.

Ahrefs



Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Features

  • Backlink alerts data and new keywords: Get an alert when your site is linked to or discussed in blogs, forums, comments, or when new keywords are added to a blog posting about you.
  • Intuitive interface: The intuitive design of the widget helps you see the overall health of your website and search engine ranking at a glance.
  • Site Explorer: The Site Explorer will give you an in-depth look at your site's search traffic.
  • Domain Comparison
  • Reports with charts and graphs
  • JavaScript rendering and a site audit can identify SEO issues.
  • A question explorer that provides well-crafted topic suggestions

Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

User Interface

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

  • You can see analytics from the dashboard, including search engine rankings to domain ratings, referring domains, and backlink
  • Jumping from one tool to another is easy. You can use the Keyword Explorer to find a keyword to target and then directly track your ranking with one click.
  • The website offers a tooltip helper tool that allows you to hover your mouse over something that isn't clear and get an in-depth explanation.

SEMRUSH



When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

You'll also find some other options like

  • A search bar allows you to enter a domain, keyword, or anything else you wish to explore.
  • A menu on the left side of the page provides quick links to relevant information, including marketing insights, projects, keyword analytics, and more.
  • The customer support resources located directly within the dashboard can be used to communicate with the support team or to learn about other resources such as webinars and blogs.
  • Detailed descriptions of every resource offered. This detail is beneficial for new marketers, who are just starting.

WHO WINS?

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

Rank Tracking

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

Ahrefs



The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRUSH



SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

All subscribers are given regular data updates and mobile search rankings upon subscribing

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

WHO WINS?

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword Research

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

  • It can search multiple keywords in a single search and analyze them together. At SEMrush, you also have this feature in Keyword Overview.
  • Ahrefs has a variety of keywords for different search engines, including Google, YouTube, Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, and other search engines.
  • When you click on a keyword, you can see its search volume and keyword difficulty, but also other keywords related to it, which you didn't use.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

The Keyword Magic Tool also lets you to:

  • Show performance metrics by keyword
  • Search results are based on both broad and exact keyword matches.
  • Show data like search volume, trends, keyword difficulty, and CPC.
  • Show the first 100 Google search results for any keyword.
  • Identify SERP Features and Questions related to each keyword
  • SEMrush has released a new Keyword Gap Tool that uncovers potentially useful keyword opportunities for you, including both paid and organic keywords.

WHO WINS?

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Competitor Analysis

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

AHREFS



Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

WHO WINS?

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

Pricing

Ahrefs

  • Lite Monthly: $99/month
  • Standard Monthly: $179/month
  • Annually Lite: $990/year
  • Annually Standard: $1790/year

SEMRUSH

  • Pro Plan: $119.95/month
  • Guru Plan:$229.95/month
  • Business Plan: $449.95/month

Which SEO tool should you choose for digital marketing?

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Consider choosing Ahrefs if you

  • Like friendly and clean interface
  • Searching for simple keyword suggestions

  • Want to get more keywords for different search engines like Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, Baidu, and more

 

Consider SEMrush if you:

  • Want more marketing and SEO features
  • Need competitor analysis tool
  • Need to keep your backlinks profile clean
  • Looking for more keyword suggestions for Google

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9729. How to Modernize Bank Without Taking Its Payment Systems Offline

Senior Solution Architect, Diebold Nixdorf. 16 years in secure payments, ATM/POS and digital banking. MSc AI candidate.

Senior Solution Architect, Diebold Nixdorf. 16 years in secure payments, ATM/POS and digital banking. MSc AI candidate.

Senior Solution Architect, Diebold Nixdorf. 16 years in secure payments, ATM/POS and digital banking. MSc AI candidate.

Every bank I have worked with has a system nobody wants to touch.

Sometimes it is a mainframe core banking platform written in COBOL. Sometimes it is a card switch that has been processing ISO 8583 messages reliably for twenty years. Sometimes it is a batch file job that runs at 2 a.m. and that exactly one engineer understands. These systems are old, but they are not broken. They move real money every second.

And yet the business wants mobile apps, open banking APIs, real-time payments and cloud analytics. The question is never "should we modernize?" The question is "how do we modernize without taking the ATM network offline on a Friday payday?"

After roughly sixteen years building ATM, POS and digital banking middleware for banks across the Middle East, Asia and Europe, here is what I have seen actually work.

The tempting plan is to replace the old core in one program. It rarely goes well. Large core replacements have a long public history of delays, outages and customers locked out of their accounts. The reasons repeat:

The alternative is incremental modernization. Less exciting, far more survivable.

Before writing new code, build an inventory of every point where systems talk to each other: protocols (ISO 8583, SWIFT MT/MX, ISO 20022, flat files, SOAP, proprietary TCP), message volumes, peak times, and who owns each interface.

In most banks this map reveals a "spaghetti" of point-to-point links. The ATM switch talks directly to the core. The mobile app calls a SOAP service that calls another SOAP service that writes to a shared database. Every new channel added another direct connection.

You cannot modernize what you have not mapped. You also cannot secure it.

The single most valuable move is introducing a governed integration layer between channels and back-end systems. This can be an API gateway plus a payment middleware or message broker, depending on the flow.

With the layer in place, use the strangler fig pattern: move one business flow at a time from legacy to new, while the rest keeps running untouched.

For each flow, run the new path in shadow mode first: send traffic to both systems, compare results, and only switch over when mismatches are near zero. Keep the routing switch reversible for weeks, not hours.

Integration layers are where security quietly degrades. Patterns I see repeatedly:

This matters well beyond one bank. In the United States, CISA identifies financial services as critical infrastructure, and regulators such as the FFIEC and OCC have repeatedly flagged third-party and legacy integration risk. As U.S. banks connect older cores to real-time rails like the Federal Reserve's FedNow Service and to ISO 20022 messaging, the integration layer becomes the front line of payment security.

During migration, two systems may each believe they own the truth. Automate reconciliation between legacy and new ledgers daily at minimum, and in near real time for payment flows. Every mismatch is either a migration bug or a hidden business rule you did not know about. Both are worth finding before customers do.

Teams celebrate when the new system goes live and forget to decommission the old path. Two systems running forever means double the attack surface and double the cost. For each migrated flow, define:

Legacy banking systems are not the enemy. They are proof that something worked for decades. Modernization succeeds when it respects that, puts a disciplined integration layer between old and new, moves one flow at a time, and treats security and reconciliation as part of the design.

The banks that get this right do not make headlines. Their customers simply never notice the migration happened. That is the goal.

Senior Solution Architect, Diebold Nixdorf. 16 years in secure payments, ATM/POS and digital banking. MSc AI candidate.
