#9728. Fusionist Exploit: Bridge Minter Prints Unbacked ACE

Posted on Nov 22 • Originally published at panda-security.xyz

Originally published at Fusionist Exploit: Bridge Minter Prints Unbacked ACE

On 22 November 2026, an externally owned account with minting rights on Fusionist's ACE token bridge began creating unbacked ACE on BNB Smart Chain. By 20:28:02 UTC, the ACE token contract reported a total supply of about 10.02 quintillion. A public archive read of the same contract, in the block before the first mint of the day, showed a supply of 53,734,729.81 ACE. This is a defensive account of a public incident, not a how-to.

Blockaid flagged the event at 19:08:28 UTC as "a privileged token-bridge minter" minting unbacked ACE and selling it for USDT, with about $1.04 million extracted "so far," and said the attack was still going. Fusionist has not published a loss figure of its own. Independently, we counted 801,691.45 USDT arriving at one of the three addresses Blockaid named; CryptoWatchDesk published the same collector total. We have not independently verified later figures that put the haul higher.

Fusionist is a blockchain game. ACE is its token. On BNB Smart Chain the token contract is 0xc27A7191…5def4, an ACEToken with 18 decimals. New ACE on that chain is minted through Fusionist's RemoteTokenBridge at 0x9d0698D9…55915. A token bridge is supposed to mint on one chain only when the same tokens are locked on another. Sunday's mints were not matched by any lock that Fusionist has described.

Every mint we observed was sent by the same EOA, 0x3f104521…0f34e, directly to the bridge. The first activity on this window was at 17:55:40 UTC. From 18:02:43 UTC, the bridge minted to a second EOA that Blockaid also named, 0x1029aa6A…e12C5. CyberSIXT and CryptoWatchDesk, reading the same chain, start their mint count at that 55 million ACE transfer. We counted 25 successful mints to that receiver between 18:02:43 and 20:28:02 UTC, which matches CryptoWatchDesk's later tally.

The amounts grew quickly. After early mints of 50 million to 55 million ACE, the same receiver was credited 800 million, then batches of 1.2 billion — including Blockaid's example transaction, 0x7b4c4546…cf14b, at 18:41:37 UTC in block 135,128,849. A run of 2 billion ACE mints followed. At 19:05:20 UTC the bridge minted 5 trillion ACE in 0xc77068f6…8571e; at 19:25:01 and 19:45:54 UTC, 10 quadrillion each time. At 20:28:02 UTC, 58 minutes after Fusionist's public warning, it minted 10 quintillion ACE in 0xb5dccc1d…3c3b5. We found no further ACE mints on this contract through 23:13 UTC.

The 25 mints to the Blockaid-named receiver add up to about 10.020 quintillion ACE, which accounts for essentially all of the post-incident supply. The same minter also created 365,000,009 ACE in 32 other mints, mostly in two bursts at 17:55 and 18:18 UTC across 14 other addresses. Gate later used 17:55 UTC as the start of its ACE/USDT rollback window. We do not have Fusionist's word on whether those earlier credits were routine or part of the same incident.

Each of the 57 mint transactions calls the same selector, 0x156e29f6. The Ethereum Signature Database records that selector as mint(address,uint256,uint256). In Blockaid's example transaction, the arguments are the receiver 0x1029aa6A…e12C5, the integer 8, and 1,200,000,000 ACE, matching the Transfer from the zero address in the same receipt. We have not established what 8 represents in this bridge. The snippet below is only a sketch of the authorization pattern, not the project's source.

The ACE contract itself did not have to be broken for this to work. It minted because the bridge, which it treats as a minter, asked it to. The unanswered question is how 0x3f104521…0f34e became an accepted minter: a taken Fusionist key, or an address the attacker managed to enroll. Blockaid and Fusionist have not said. In the roughly 25 hours before 17:55 UTC, we found no other ACE mints on this token contract.

A Supremacy audit dated 26 August 2024, still hosted on Fusionist's bridge site and scoped to this same RemoteTokenBridge address, had already flagged centralized risk as an informational finding. It noted that key bridge features were controlled by EOA privilege accounts and recommended multi-signature or MPC wallets, a timelock, and, over a longer horizon, governance. That finding does not prove which role Sunday's caller held. It does show that single-key mint authority was a known design choice.

We re-read the token supply, the mint logs, and the Blockaid example transaction on public BNB Smart Chain endpoints, including an archive node for historical totalSupply. In block 135,122,722, immediately before the 17:55 burst, supply was 53,734,729.81168212 ACE. After the 20:28 mint, in block 135,143,036, it was about 10.020005029652 quintillion ACE, in line with CryptoWatchDesk's later check. The example transaction's only token logs are the bridge mint and the ACE Transfer from the zero address. The contracts did what a privileged mint call is meant to do.

Market pages still quote an official ACE cap of 147 million. That figure is not the BNB Chain totalSupply we read, and it was already obsolete on this chain once the large mints landed.

Blockaid named a third exploiter address, 0xb335cd87…019b5. Between 18:02:43 and 20:28:02 UTC, that address received 25 USDT transfers totaling 801,691.45 USDT. All but the last came from a swap contract at 0x8f10b468…3f996. CryptoWatchDesk counted the same 801,691 USDT at this collector and said it had not traced the rest of Blockaid's $1.04 million mid-attack figure. Onchain Lens later wrote that $1.87 million had been routed across wallets, chains, and Tornado Cash. We have not independently confirmed that larger path, and Fusionist has not released an official total.

USDT receipts shrank as the minted amounts exploded, which is what you would expect once on-chain ACE/USDT liquidity had been sold into. The 5 trillion ACE mint at 19:05 UTC was followed by 16,695.95 USDT at the collector; the two 10-quadrillion mints produced 5,076.08 and 359.20 USDT; the 10 quintillion mint, 1,515.54 USDT.

At 19:30:20 UTC, Fusionist's account @fusionistio posted a security alert: it was investigating "an apparent ongoing exploit involving ACE on BSC" and asked holders to pause ACE transfers, trades, and bridging on BSC until further notice. As of this writing, the team has not published a root cause, a loss figure, or a reimbursement plan, and it has not said whether ACE on other chains is affected.

Gate posted at 20:54 UTC that it had detected an abnormal mint of 5 trillion ACE from the ACE bridge — the size of the 19:05 transaction — and that its security team had confirmed the bridge was exploited. It said it would roll back ACE/USDT spot trades between 17:55 and 19:15 UTC, treat later deposits of the newly minted tokens as fork coins if the project later calls them invalid, and settle ACE perpetual futures at 04:00 UTC on 24 November. Holders on other venues should read those venues' own notices.

A privileged minter is a money printer. Access control on mint is the control that keeps one chain's supply tied to a lock on another. If a single EOA can call that function without a cap, a delay, or a second signature, then a stolen or mis-assigned key can inflate supply until liquidity is gone. The same class of failure appears when a bridge trusts a signer more than it can actually constrain, as in the Ankr Bridge forged-receipt case.

A warning is not a circuit breaker. Fusionist's pause request at 19:30 UTC was the right public message for holders. It did not revoke the minter. Two 10-quadrillion mints and a 10-quintillion mint still landed afterward. An emergency path has to take minting offline — by revoking the role, pausing the token, or enforcing a hard supply cap — rather than asking counterparties to stop trading.

Audit findings about EOA roles age badly if they stay informational. The 2024 review of this exact RemoteTokenBridge already recommended moving privileged keys off a plain EOA. Sunday's transactions do not prove that recommendation was ignored, but they are the outcome it exists to prevent. For a pre-launch pass over bridges, minters and admin keys, use a smart contract security checklist that treats role design as in-scope. The recent Chainflip vault drain is a reminder that a valid authorization, once the wrong party can produce it, will mint tokens or move funds exactly as designed.

Follow Fusionist only through official channels, beginning with @fusionistio. Until the team says otherwise, do not transfer, trade, or bridge ACE on BNB Smart Chain. If you hold ACE on an exchange, read that venue's incident notice before depositing or withdrawing. Do not connect a wallet, sign a "migration," or send funds to anyone offering a refund.

Sunday's ACE inflation on BNB Smart Chain did not require a broken Transfer hook. It required a mint call that Fusionist's own bridge would accept. The on-chain record is consistent across Blockaid, CyberSIXT, CryptoWatchDesk and our reread: one EOA, one bridge, a supply that jumped from tens of millions to about 10.02 quintillion, and hundreds of thousands of USDT at the collector Blockaid named. What remains open is how that EOA obtained the role, how much was taken beyond the collector we could count, and what Fusionist will do for holders.

If you are shipping a token bridge, a cross-chain minter, or any contract that lets a privileged key create supply, talk to our team or review audit pricing before that key can print against a live pool.

#9727. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

#9726. What Happens to Your Digital Accounts After a Chargeback?

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Your issuing bank will happily hand your 50 USD back. What the representative on the phone will rarely mention is that once those funds are clawed back, the merchant on the other side of the trade holds sweeping contractual rights over your account. When that merchant happens to run your cloud storage, your smart home, your decade-old gaming library, or your daily ride to work, a minor billing victory can turn into a painful digital lockout overnight.

After 25 years in traditional banking, I cringe every time I hear social media finance gurus repeat their favorite piece of lazy advice: "If customer support gives you a hard time about a refund, just call your credit card company and file a chargeback." People treat the bank dispute button like a VIP customer service hotline. It is nothing of the sort. Inside the plumbing of global card rails, a chargeback is a forced financial extraction. You are asking your bank to reach directly into a merchant's settlement balance, pull the cash back over the card network, trigger a punitive dispute fee, and log a blemish against their compliance metrics with Visa or Mastercard.

Do that to a neighborhood dry cleaner and they might ban you from the shop. Do that to Apple, Google, Sony, Valve, Microsoft, Amazon, or Uber over a 20 USD subscription renewal, and you are rolling the dice with automated risk engines that control far more than a single receipt. At best, your profile gets hit with an unpaid balance lock or a payment verification hold; at worst, if the platform flags the reversal as payment abuse or unauthorized activity, you can win a 20 USD battle at your bank only to lose access to thousands of dollars in purchased media, connected devices, or cloud workflows.

To understand why tech platforms treat bank disputes so seriously, you have to understand the legal and operational chasm between a refund and a chargeback. During a standard refund, the merchant voluntarily pushes money back to your card over the payment rails. During a chargeback, your issuing bank forcibly reverses the transaction through the card network's dispute machinery, bypassing the merchant's checkout support entirely.

Consumers often assume that when their bank rules in their favor, the case is closed and the merchant has to respect the verdict. That is a costly misunderstanding of how commercial law works. Your bank adjudicates whether you owe the money on your monthly card statement; the tech platform adjudicates whether you are allowed to use its servers under its terms of service. When you pull the trigger on a dispute, your money and your account standing can quickly start moving in opposite directions.

In the United States, consumer banking protections are remarkably strong on paper. For credit cards, the Fair Credit Billing Act (implemented through Regulation Z) gives you the legal right to challenge billing errors and unauthorized charges. According to the CFPB's official credit card dispute rules, as long as you send written notice within 60 calendar days after the error first appeared on your statement, the card issuer must investigate and pause collection on the disputed charge (often issuing a temporary credit) while the case plays out. Debit cards carry separate protections for unauthorized electronic fund transfers under Regulation E's error resolution framework.

Here is the catch that catches everyday users off guard. Regulation Z and Regulation E bind your bank, not the merchant. Zero federal statutes force a private corporation to keep extending services to a customer who just reversed a settled payment.

Worse yet, consumers increasingly lean on bank disputes for what the payments industry calls first-party fraud, or "friendly fraud." According to Mastercard's 2026 chargeback outlook, global chargeback volume is projected to reach 334 million disputes annually by 2028, while merchants report that 21% of chargebacks are linked to first-party fraud, ranging from unrecognized or forgotten charges to intentional misuse of the dispute process. Separate Mastercard-sponsored research with Javelin found that for 75% of disputes, consumers go straight to their card issuer without contacting the merchant first. Because issuing banks often find it cheaper to credit small disputes automatically than to investigate them manually, cardholders get lulled into thinking the tactic is consequence-free.

Of course, if a thief steals your physical wallet or hijacks your account, you must call your bank immediately and freeze the card. My warning here applies to using bank disputes as a casual shortcut to resolve everyday billing friction with ecosystems you cannot afford to lose.

If you want to know why a trillion-dollar company will freeze purchases or restrict an account over a 19.99 USD charge, stop looking at the customer support department and look at the treasury and risk desk. Every card transaction travels along a four-party rail: you (the cardholder), your issuing bank (such as Chase or Capital One), the card network (Visa or Mastercard), and the merchant's acquiring bank or payment processor (such as Stripe, Adyen, or J.P. Morgan Merchant Services).

When you initiate a chargeback, a costly chain reaction hits the merchant's back office:

Put yourself in the shoes of a platform risk officer looking at that math. A customer who files a 20 USD chargeback has just inflicted over 100 USD in combined direct and operational losses on the company. From a pure risk-management standpoint, letting an account rack up bank reversals unchecked makes zero financial sense.

The direct fees are only half the story. The deeper reason merchants aggressively police chargebacks is card network compliance enforcement. Visa and Mastercard track dispute and fraud ratios across every merchant portfolio on their rails.

In recent years, Visa overhauled its legacy compliance rules and consolidated five separate fraud and dispute tracks into a single framework: the Visa Acquirer Monitoring Program (VAMP). Under the official VAMP threshold schedule, Visa calculates a merchant's monthly ratio by combining TC40 fraud notices and TC15 non-fraud disputes divided by total settled card-not-present VisaNet transactions, with the U.S. Excessive Merchant threshold tightening to 1.5% (alongside at least 1,500 monthly combined fraud and dispute notices) in April 2026. Even if a merchant fights a chargeback and wins, that dispute still counts toward their monthly monitoring ratio.

Mastercard enforces a parallel framework called the Excessive Chargeback Program (ECP). As outlined in Stripe's card network monitoring guide, crossing both the 1.5% rate and 100-chargeback monthly count places a merchant into official remediation, with escalating monthly fines kicking in from the second consecutive month unless the ratio drops back below threshold. Payment processors simultaneously protect themselves from elevated dispute activity by holding a portion of a merchant's payouts in fixed or rolling reserves, as detailed in Stripe's merchant reserve policies.

Crossing a Visa or Mastercard monitoring threshold does not automatically terminate a merchant or blacklist the business overnight; the programs are built around mandatory remediation plans and escalating fees first. However, if a smaller vendor fails to bring its dispute levels down in time, the card network can eventually stop processing its payments, or its acquiring bank may terminate the account. As documented in Stripe's guide to terminated merchant files, once an acquirer terminates a merchant that meets specific network reporting criteria, such as Mastercard's MATCH Reason Code 04 (exceeding a 1% monthly Mastercard chargeback ratio and 5,000 USD in chargebacks within the same calendar month) or Visa's VMSS thresholds, the acquirer must report the business to those five-year high-risk databases, making it nearly impossible to open a new card-processing account elsewhere.

Even for giants like Sony, Apple, or Amazon, keeping ratios clean across dozens of regional merchant descriptors requires tight automated controls. Depending on how their fraud models classify a reversal, their systems will either lock new spending until the unpaid balance is cleared or quarantine the account for a security review.

Platforms do not react identically to every chargeback, and it helps to separate routine billing enforcement from worst-case account bans. Routinely, a single reversed payment creates an unpaid balance on your profile, revokes the specific item you disputed, or pauses new purchases until you settle the tab or verify your card. Contractually, however, every major tech ecosystem reserves broad authority to suspend or terminate accounts, and when an automated fraud model classifies a chargeback as unauthorized activity or payment abuse, the blast radius can hit your entire digital profile.

Gaming platforms enforce some of the strictest automated chargeback rules in the consumer economy, though each handles the boundary between a single revoked purchase and a full account lock differently.

Sony leaves very little wiggle room in its public rules. Under the PlayStation Network account debt and suspension policy, because a bank reversal can signal suspected fraud or an account takeover, Sony suspends the PSN account (or console) to investigate, displaying error codes WS-37368-7 or WS-116367-4 and restricting access to online services. If there was no lawful right to a refund, your PSN profile remains suspended until you repay the owed balance through Sony's recovery form, cutting you off from PlayStation Store purchases, online multiplayer, and PSN-authenticated features in the meantime.

Microsoft separates baseline chargeback handling from fraud enforcement across Xbox and Windows services. While Microsoft provides an official Xbox digital game refund portal for standard refund requests, bypassing Microsoft via your bank triggers Section 9.g of the Microsoft Services Agreement: Microsoft deems you to have canceled the service as of the original payment date and is authorized to immediately cancel that service and revoke the content provided for that payment. That is the routine baseline. However, if Xbox's risk systems determine that a chargeback or refund pattern crosses into fraudulent marketplace theft, Xbox Safety enforcement can escalate to temporary or permanent account and console bans, and Section 4.b.iv of the Services Agreement warns that permanent closure can forfeit your content licenses, memberships, and Microsoft account balances.

Think about how much of your daily digital routine runs through your Apple Account (formerly Apple ID). Under the Apple Media Services Terms and Conditions, you remain personally liable for any uncollected amounts, and Apple reserves broad authority to suspend or terminate access to its services or your Apple Account if you breach the agreement.

In everyday practice, Apple's documentation points to two distinct tiers of friction. If a failed or reversed payment simply leaves an unpaid order on your profile, Apple's unpaid balance support guide states that you might be unable to make new purchases, download free apps, or use subscriptions (and as noted in Apple's Mac App Store troubleshooting guide, an unpaid order can also block you from downloading or updating apps). In these routine unpaid-balance cases, manual intervention is not required: you can clear the balance yourself by adding a new valid payment method, which Apple charges automatically, or by redeeming an Apple Gift Card and applying the credit to the unpaid order in your purchase history.

However, if a chargeback or repeated billing dispute triggers an anti-fraud lock that disables your purchasing privileges outright, self-service card updates will no longer fix the problem. As shown in Apple's disabled Media & Purchases recovery guide, seeing the alert that your Media & Purchases account has been disabled means you have to request reactivation directly through Apple Support.

Google routes consumer and business billing through a shared hub: your Google Payments profile. As explained in Google's payments center documentation, that profile stores the cards, receipts, and recurring subscriptions behind Google Play, YouTube, Google One storage, hardware orders, and business tools.

A consumer chargeback does not automatically wipe out your Google Account or shut off Gmail on the spot. Instead, under the Google Pay and Google Payments U.S. Terms and Google's declined-transaction rules, when unusual or suspicious payment activity flags your payments profile, Google can block new purchases until you complete identity and payment verification, which may involve confirming a 6-digit temporary charge code or uploading images of a government ID and the payment card. If you also run ad campaigns on that account, Google Ads' billing suspension policy explicitly warns that instructing your bank to reverse a legitimate ad balance may result in your Google Ads account being paused or suspended.

For everyday users, the real danger of an unresolved payments-profile lock is the delayed domino effect on cloud storage. Under Google One's renewal and cancellation policies, if auto-renewal fails on your storage plan, Google provides a seven-day grace period to update your payment information. If a locked payments profile or unresolved billing dispute keeps your plan from renewing past that window and your usage sits above the free 15 GB quota, your Google Account stays accessible, but Google Photos stops backing up videos and pictures, Google Drive blocks new uploads and Workspace file creation, and Gmail stops sending and receiving messages, returning incoming emails to the sender. Leave an account over quota for two years or longer, and Google states your content may be deleted.

Amazon is no longer just a retailer that ships cardboard boxes to your porch; it also runs media libraries and smart-home devices tied to the same login. On routine marketplace disputes, Amazon's A-to-z Guarantee rules explicitly note that filing a credit card chargeback disqualifies that order from A-to-z Guarantee refund coverage, and ordinary payment declines usually just pause pending orders until you supply another card.

The stakes jump sharply, however, if a reversed charge or disputed card causes Amazon's risk models to flag your profile for unusual payment activity. Under Amazon's Conditions of Use, the company reserves broad discretion to refuse service or terminate accounts. More specifically, Amazon's Account on Hold policy states in plain English that when unusual payment activity triggers a temporary security hold on your account, your access to all Amazon services is also placed on hold during the review, explicitly listing Amazon Prime, Amazon Music, Kindle, and devices like Alexa and Ring. Until you sign into Amazon's secure portal and submit its verification form with the requested supporting attachments, your shopping account and connected digital services stay frozen together.

Uber illustrates a similar single-wallet bottleneck in daily transit and food delivery. Under Uber's U.S. Terms of Use, Uber retains sole discretion to deny access to or terminate any of its services at any time. In day-to-day operations, when a failed or reversed payment leaves an unpaid balance on your account, Uber's rider pending-amount rules and the matching Uber Eats outstanding-charge policy warn that you may be unable to request a ride or place a food order until you settle the pending charge in the app with a valid payment method (or arrange cash payment where supported).

Stepping back and looking at this friction through the lens of payment architecture reveals a striking irony. For decades, traditional bankers criticized cryptocurrency protocols because on-chain transactions are final and irreversible, whereas legacy credit cards offer consumer reversibility.

Yet in practice, credit card settlement finality is an illusion that encourages digital feudalism. When you swipe a Visa card, the merchant receives provisional funds within a couple of business days, but the transaction lacks true finality for months while card-network dispute windows remain open. Because centralized platforms cannot fully trust the finality of legacy fiat payment rails, they protect their balance sheets by tying your digital identity, subscriptions, and device ecosystems to a single revocable login.

In the crypto and Web3 world, we live by a simple rule: not your keys, not your coins. If you leave your digital assets on a centralized exchange, you do not hold bearer Bitcoin or stablecoins; you hold a revocable database entry that the exchange can freeze the moment a compliance or billing review flares up.

The exact same custody trap governs Web2 walled gardens. Not your servers, not your files. Even when you click the purchase button on an e-book, Amazon's Kindle Store terms of use explicitly state that digital content is licensed to you, not sold. When you bundle your primary email address, your cloud drive, your smart-home cameras, and thousands of dollars of revocable media licenses inside the same single sign-on profile that processes your credit card, you hand the platform enormous leverage. Your bank can force the merchant to return 50 USD, and the merchant retains the contractual power to freeze your billing profile, halt subscriptions, or, in severe enforcement cases, cut off access to thousands of dollars in licensed media.

In commercial banking, putting all of your operational liquidity and custody inside a single counterparty that can freeze your operations over a minor billing dispute is called concentration risk. No competent corporate treasurer would allow it, yet everyday consumers build their digital lives that way by default.

If you want to protect your money from bad billing without handing Big Tech unnecessary leverage over your accounts, follow these five operational rules.

If an unfamiliar storefront scams you on a pair of shoes from a random social media ad, file a chargeback without hesitation. However, if you are fighting a 30 USD charge from Apple, Google, Amazon, Sony, or Valve, treat the bank dispute button as a last resort. Exhaust the platform's internal refund escalation channels, reach out to executive customer relations, or file a formal complaint with the Better Business Bureau or your state Attorney General's consumer protection division first. Track your 60-day statutory bank deadline on the calendar so you never forfeit your legal rights under Regulation Z or Regulation E, but push the merchant to resolve the billing error internally whenever an essential account is on the line.

The cleanest way to win a billing dispute is to stop an unwanted charge at the authorization gate before the money ever settles. Once a charge settles, reversing it through your bank creates a chargeback; stopping an unwanted renewal at authorization simply triggers a routine "payment declined, please update your billing method" notice.

If you have thousands of dollars invested in a PlayStation, Steam, Xbox, or Apple library, leaving a live credit card or PayPal billing agreement on file means an accidental click, a child's in-game purchase, or a forgotten renewal can quickly turn into a high-stakes billing mess.

Instead, fund those wallets with prepaid store gift cards purchased from reputable retailers and remove live cards where possible. That way, the platform cannot pull more than the prepaid balance sitting in your wallet. Keep one practical rule in mind: under Apple's payment method removal policy, you must keep at least one payment method on file if you maintain active subscriptions like iCloud+, owe an unpaid balance, or serve as a Family Sharing organizer with purchase sharing enabled. Even then, keeping your Apple Account funded with gift cards helps ensure your prepaid balance absorbs routine charges before a backup card is touched.

Stop using the same Google or Apple account that holds your tax returns, family photo archives, and two-factor authentication recovery emails to test sketchy app trials or shared household entertainment. Build an air gap between your core infrastructure and your discretionary spending. Keep your primary email and cloud storage on a clean, dedicated account paid by a reliable card used strictly for storage infrastructure, and maintain a separate secondary account for media purchases, trials, and gaming.

Never confuse cloud syncing with an independent backup. If a payment verification hold or account suspension disrupts your Google, Microsoft, or Apple services tomorrow morning, any document or photo sitting exclusively inside a single cloud drive is exposed to single-provider risk. Keep local, encrypted backups of your critical documents, family photos, and password vaults on external drives you physically control, and make sure your two-factor authentication recovery codes are never stored solely inside the email inbox they are meant to unlock.

If you are reading this because you already filed a bank dispute and ran into a restricted PlayStation, Steam, Apple, or Google account, stop panicking and do not file a second dispute. Restoring access requires a careful reconciliation sequence between your bank and the merchant:

Consumer chargeback rights remain an essential safeguard against criminal fraud and rogue merchants. Use them without hesitation when a stranger steals your card details or a fly-by-night storefront takes your money and vanishes. Just understand how the payment rails and platform contracts actually interact before you fire that weapon at an ecosystem holding the keys to your digital life.

#9724. AWS + Docker CI Need Isolated Email Fixtures

Email verification tests are often the first thing to become unreliable when a CI pipeline starts running in parallel. One build reads another build's message, a retry finds an already-consumed token, or cleanup removes the inbox before the failure can be investigated.

I have had better results by treating an email fixture like a short-lived infrastructure resource. Each build gets an identity, a bounded lifetime, and an artifact trail. The pattern works in Docker locally and in AWS-hosted CI, without turning the test suite into a shared mailbox scavenger hunt.

A shared inbox creates hidden coupling between jobs. The test code may ask for the newest verification email, but "newest" is not the same as "mine" when four pull requests are active. Timing then becomes the accidental coordination system.

The failures is usually reported as a flaky test, even though the underlying problem is ownership. A build needs to know which inbox it created, which messages belong to that inbox, and whether the message was consumed already. A subject prefix helps, but it is not a complete boundary by itself. The real fix are ownership rules, not another sleep statement.

I also avoid putting real user data into these fixtures. If a team uses a disposable mail address for a controlled test account, the address should be scoped to the build and never reused for production workflows.

Start with a build identifier that is safe for logs and URLs:

Store the returned address and message identifier in the job workspace, not in a global environment variable shared by later jobs. A job should be able to answer three questions from its own files:

This is an execution boundary, not just a naming convention. The API client should reject a message whose fixture ID does not match the current build. In practice, that check caught more cross-job contamination than increasing polling delays. It is easy to loose the lease context when a helper hides the request details, so keep it visible in the test output.

For a deeper look at the other side of this problem, I keep deletion proof for temporary inbox tests in the same review checklist. Creation and cleanup are one lifecycle, so they should be observed together.

In local development, put the fixture adapter and the application under test on a private Docker network. The test container receives only the adapter URL and its fixture ID:

Do not use depends_on as proof that an email is available. It only controls startup order. The test still needs a bounded poll with a correlation ID, and it should report the last observed message IDs when the poll expires. Otherwise the logs say only "timeout", which is not enough to fix the issue.

The same boundary works in CI. Each parallel job starts its own adapter or requests a unique namespace from a shared adapter. The seperate choice depends on cost and throughput: isolated processes are easier to reason about, while a shared service needs strict tenant filtering and quotas. The logs should be clear enought that an on-call can follow one build without opening every job.

When this runs on AWS, retain a small diagnostic bundle on failure. It can include the fixture lease, sanitized message metadata, the test report, Docker logs, and the correlation ID. Avoid storing message bodies if they can contain tokens or personal data.

For an ephemeral runner, upload the bundle before the cleanup trap runs. A runner can dissapear quickly after a failed step, so the trap must do useful work in a small window:

The bucket needs a short retention policy and restricted access. Do not put tokens in object names, and do not assume that a deleted local file means the uploaded artifact is gone. This is where teams often get a bit surprised: observability can quietly become data retention. Keep the cleanup path simple and repeatable, even if it feels slightly over careful.

A typed client in the test harness also helps keep the states explicit. A typed decision boundary in the test client is a useful model for separating pending, received, expired, and rejected states. The exact language is less important than making an expired lease impossible to treat as a valid message.

Long enough for the slowest supported CI region and retry path, with a hard upper limit. Pick the value from observed pipeline timings, then add a margin. Never let an abandoned job keep an inbox forever.

Usually yes within one test attempt, but give each retry a new correlation ID. Reusing a message token across attempts can hide a race and makes the test result harder to replay.

Log IDs, timestamps, state transitions, and counts. Redact addresses and message contents unless a controlled debugging mode explicitly requires them. A temp mailid in a log can still be sensitive if it is live.

This approach adds a little setup, but it removes a large amount of mystery. CI becomes a sequence of owned resources: create, verify, observe, and release. That is calmer than asking a shared inbox what happened after the pipeline is already red.

#9722. Pulse Break: a 60-second camera check-in between focus blocks

This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge

Pulse Break is a small terminal app for the gap between two blocks of focused work. You run it, look at your camera for a minute, and the SmartSpectra SDK reads your pulse and breathing rate from the video. At the end, Pulse Break compares those two numbers with your own recent check-ins. If you are clearly running warmer than your usual, it suggests a five-minute break before the next block. If not, it tells you to keep going.

The comparison is against you, not against a chart. A pulse of 80 means different things for different people, so the app asks only one question: is this check-in noticeably above what is normal for me?

I work on biosignal input at Somach Systems, where the sensors are EMG electrodes on the skin. A tool that gets pulse and breathing from the webcam already on the desk, with nothing to wear, was the part of this challenge I wanted to try.

The demo runs on a recorded clip of me (from 2026-11-02, sound removed), not on a live camera. The SDK reads the clip at the clip's own frame rate, so the readings arrive the way they would from a webcam. On the left is the footage the SDK reads; on the right is the app's terminal, drawn live from the SDK's metrics and lined up with the clip's clock. Nothing in the terminal panel was edited. The two earlier check-ins in the history at the end are also recorded clips of me.

A 60-second check-in for the gap between two focus blocks. You look at your camera, the Presage SmartSpectra SDK reads your pulse and breathing rate from the video, and Pulse Break compares the result with your own recent check-ins. If you are running clearly warmer than your usual, it suggests a five-minute break before the next block. Otherwise it tells you to keep going.

It is a terminal app built on the SDK's Node.js binding. Everything it shows comes from the SDK's live metrics while the check-in runs.

Demo video (runs on a recorded clip of me, see below): https://youtu.be/Xldyvg1omy0

Setup is in the README: Node.js 20.12 or later, npm install, a free Presage API key in .env, then node src/cli.mjs. To try it without a camera, node src/cli.mjs --video your-clip.mp4 reads a recording of yourself instead.

Signals used: pulse rate and breathing rate, plus the SDK's chest-motion trace and its per-frame readiness hints.

While a check-in runs, the dashboard redraws up to ten times a second:

When the time is up, it takes the median of the steady pulse readings and the median breathing rate, and compares them with the median of your last seven check-ins:

The first two check-ins only build your usual. The thresholds are round numbers chosen to be easy to explain, not clinical cut-offs, and they live in one small file with unit tests.

The integration is in src/session.mjs. It uses the Node SDK (@smartspectra/node-sdk 3.5.0) with requestedMetrics: [...breathingMetrics, ...cardioMetrics], then useCamera(CameraSelection.default) for a live check-in or useFile() for a recording. The validationStatus event drives the readiness line. Each metrics packet goes through decodeMetrics, and the app reads cardio.pulseRate (value, stable flag, confidence), breathing.rate and breathing.upperTrace.

Best Thoughtful Real-World Use. The need is small on purpose: a quick way to notice, between two blocks of work, whether you are running warmer than usual, using only the webcam that is already there. I designed for that: one command, one minute, one line of advice, numbers compared only with your own, a consent question before every check-in, and nothing saved except two numbers per check-in.

#9721. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

 


Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

What is Sellfy?

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Features

Sellfy includes:

Online Store

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Product hosting

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Embed options

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Payments and security

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.


Marketing and analytics tools

The Sellfy platform includes marketing and analytics tools to help you manage your online store. You can send email product updates and collect newsletter subscribers through the platform. With Sellfy, you can also offer discount codes and product upsells, as well as create and track Facebook and Twitter ads for your store. The software's analytics dashboard will help you track your best-performing products, generated revenue, traffic channels, top locations, and overall store performance.

Integrations

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Pricing and Premium Plan Features

Sellfy Review: Pros and Cons

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

Pros

  • It takes only a few minutes to set up an online store and begin selling products.
  • You can sell your products on a single storefront, even if you are selling multiple product types.
  • Sellfy supports selling a variety of product types, including physical items, digital goods, subscriptions, and print-on-demand products.

  • Sellfy offers a free plan for those who want to test out the features before committing to a paid plan.
  • You get paid the same day you make a sale. Sellfy doesn't delay your funds as some other payment processors do. 
  • Print-on-demand services are available directly from your store, so you can sell merchandise to fans without setting up an integration. 
  • You can conduct all store-related activities via the mobile app and all online stores have mobile responsive designs.
  • Everything you need to make your website is included, including a custom domain name hosting, security for your files, and the ability to customize your store
  • The file security features can help you protect your digital property by allowing you to put PDF stamps, set download limits, and SSL encryption.
  • Sellfy provides unlimited support.
  • Sellfy provides simple and intuitive tax and VAT configuration settings.
  • Marketing strategies include coupons, email marketing, upselling, tracking pixels, and cart abandonment.

Cons

  • Although the free plan is helpful, but it limits you to only 10 products.
  • Payment plans often require an upgrade if you exceed a certain sales amount per year.
  • The storefront designs are clean, but they're not unique templates for creating a completely different brand image.
  • Sellfy's branding is removed from your hosted product when you upgrade to the $49 per month Business plan.
  • The free plan does not allow for selling digital or subscription products.

Conclusion

In this article, we have taken a look at some of the biggest benefits associated with using sellfy for eCommerce. Once you compare these benefits to what you get with other platforms such as Shopify, you should find that it is worth your time to consider sellfy for your business. #9718. Coles vs Woolworths vs ALDI: I priced the same 9 staples, and the hard part was not the scraping

Every few months someone in Australia asks which supermarket is really the cheapest. I wanted a number instead of an opinion, so I searched the same nine staples at Coles, Woolworths and ALDI on the same morning and compared them by price per kilo (or litre).

Disclosure: I built the scraper used below (Coles, Woolworths & ALDI Scraper on Apify). The matching logic works on any list of products with a name and a unit price.

Nine searches in each store (23 Nov 2026), up to 30 results each: milk, eggs, white bread, butter, a tasty cheese block, chicken breast, beef mince, spaghetti and long grain rice. One row looks like this:

The useful fields are unitPrice and unitPriceMeasure: each store already works out the price per 100 g, per kg or per litre, so a 2 kg value pack and a 500 g tray can be compared directly.

My first version took the cheapest product per kilo in each search result. ALDI won butter at $2.12/kg. The product was a tin of butter beans. Then:

So the code below keeps a product only if its name contains certain words and none of a short list of others. Every exclusion in that list is a product that really came back and really won its row before I removed it.

The basket is 2 L of milk, a dozen eggs (700 g), a 650 g loaf, 500 g of butter, a 1 kg cheese block, 1 kg each of chicken breast and beef mince, 500 g of spaghetti and 1 kg of rice.

Cheapest price per kg (per litre for milk), AUD. An asterisk means the product was on special that day.

These are online shelf prices on one day, for one delivery area, not receipts. The basket uses the cheapest matching product, which is almost always the house or value brand; if you buy brands, the answer changes. Fresh fruit and vegetables are left out on purpose: Woolworths sells bananas per piece and Coles per kilo, so they need their own conversion.

Run the same input on a schedule and keep the rows: the per-kg prices become a weekly series per store, and isOnSpecial with wasPrice shows when Coles and Woolworths rotate their half-price items. The scraper also takes whole departments ("categories": ["dairy-eggs-fridge"]) or the specials pages, if you want every product rather than nine searches.

The searches returned about 900 product rows and the runs took about a minute in total. At $0.0015 per product on the free plan that is about $1.35; Apify's free $5 monthly credit covers roughly 3,300 products, so a weekly run of this basket costs nothing.

If you have a better way to match "the same product" across stores than a list of words to exclude, I would like to hear it.

#9715. Architecting Location-Aware Sound Profiles Without Killing the Battery

It happened during a quiet afternoon meeting with a client. The room was silent, save for the hum of the projector, when suddenly my phone started blasting a notification sound. It wasn't just a simple chime; it was a loud, rhythmic alert that echoed off the walls. Every head in the room turned toward me. I fumbled to silence it, my face burning with embarrassment. I had completely forgotten to put my device into vibrate mode before walking through those double doors. That moment of friction felt entirely unnecessary.

We all live these moments. Whether it is a class, a medical appointment, or a community prayer session, the responsibility of manually managing sound profiles is a cognitive load we shouldn't have to carry. Before building Muffle, I tried various automation apps, but they usually fell into two categories: they were either overly complex behemoths that required too many permissions and background processes, or they were unreliable, failing to trigger when I walked into the building. I didn't want a complex workflow engine; I just wanted my phone to respect the silence of the room I was currently standing in.

When I started building the location-based triggering for Muffle, the immediate instinct was to poll the device's GPS coordinates at regular intervals. I quickly realized this is the fastest way to destroy battery life and get your app flagged by the Android system as a battery hog. The LocationManager API is powerful, but using it with high-frequency updates in the foreground is unsustainable. I needed a way to trigger sound profile changes based on geofencing without keeping the GPS radio active full-time.

I pivoted to the GeofencingClient within the Google Play Services library. Instead of manual polling, this API allows you to define a circular boundary and register it with the system. The OS handles the monitoring at the hardware level, essentially offloading the heavy lifting to the system's location service. When the device enters or exits the radius, the system sends an intent to my BroadcastReceiver.

kotlin val geofence = Geofence.Builder() .setRequestId("office_zone") .setCircularRegion(lat, lon, radiusMeters) .setExpirationDuration(Geofence.NEVER_EXPIRE) .setTransitionTypes(Geofence.GEOFENCE_TRANSITION_ENTER or Geofence.GEOFENCE_TRANSITION_EXIT) .build()

This architecture is efficient because the app stays dormant until the hardware signals a boundary crossing. I paired this with a Foreground Service to ensure that when the transition intent fires, the app has the permission to modify the AudioManager settings, even if the activity stack is cleared. By moving the logic from a continuous loop to an event-driven model, the impact on power consumption became negligible. It was a clear shift from "constantly checking" to "waiting for an interrupt."

What surprised me most during development was how often the GeofencingClient would fail to fire in indoor environments. I initially assumed that the GPS hardware would handle everything, but I learned the hard way that walls and building materials significantly degrade signal quality. In early testing, I would walk into my office building and the routine wouldn't trigger until I was halfway to my desk. The latency was frustrating, and my first instinct was to simply decrease the radius to increase sensitivity. That turned out to be the wrong move.

Decreasing the radius actually increased the false-positive rate because of the inherent jitter in location signals. I discovered that I needed to implement a hybrid approach. I started using a combination of FusedLocationProviderClient and some basic signal filtering to verify the location change before applying the sound profile. I also had to account for cases where the user might have location services toggled off entirely. I built an activity log inside the app to help me debug these transitions. Seeing the raw timestamps of when the system thought I entered a location versus when the sound profile actually changed helped me identify a three-second lag in the system broadcast handling. I had to refactor my BroadcastReceiver to be extremely lightweight to avoid ANR (Application Not Responding) errors during the transition, as the system imposes strict limits on how long you can hold the broadcast context.

If I were starting over, I would focus even more heavily on the "initial state" problem. What happens if the user restarts their phone while already inside a geofenced area? The GeofencingClient doesn't always automatically re-evaluate the state upon reboot if you haven't persisted the states correctly. I had to build a custom boot receiver that re-registers the geofences and queries the current location to verify if the user is already inside an active zone. It was a hidden complexity that added weeks to my development timeline but was essential for the app to function as a reliable utility.

For any developer working on background location tasks, the biggest lesson is to stop fighting the Android power management system. Don't try to keep a service alive at all costs; instead, lean into the event-based APIs provided by the system. If you try to build your own polling mechanism, the OS will eventually kill your process to save the user's battery, and you will be left with a buggy, unreliable experience. Focus on how to handle the transitions cleanly—what happens when the app wakes up, when it fails to get a signal, and when the user changes their mind. Precision in location isn't just about the GPS coordinates; it is about how you interpret those coordinates within the context of the user's actual behavior.

Automation is supposed to simplify life, not add another layer of maintenance. By treating the phone’s sound state as a reflection of physical context rather than a manual setting, you can build tools that genuinely reduce friction. Muffle started as a way to stop my phone from ringing in meetings, and it has evolved into a tool for managing context-aware silence for thousands of users. If you are interested in how I managed these background states or want to try the implementation yourself, you can find the project here: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.muffle.app

#9713. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

#9711. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly:  When it comes to English grammar, there are two Big Players that everyone knows of: the Grammarly and ProWritingAid. but you are wondering which one to choose so here we write a detail article which will help you to choose the best one for you so Let's start

What is Grammarly?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.


Features of Grammarly

  • Spelling and Word Suggestion: Grammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve it
  • Create a Personal Dictionary: The Grammarly app allows you to add words to your personal dictionary so that the same mistake isn't highlighted every time you run Grammarly.
  • Different English Style: Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.
  • Plagiarism: This feature helps you detect if a text has been plagiarized by comparing it with over eight billion web pages.
  • Wordiness: This tool will help you check your writing for long and hard-to-read sentences. It also shows you how to shorten sentences so that they are more concise.
  • Passive Voice: The program also notifies users when passive voice is used too frequently in a document.
  • Punctuations: This feature flags all incorrect and missing punctuation.
  • Repetition: The tool provides recommendations for replacing the repeated word.
  • Proposition: Grammarly identifies misplaced and confused prepositions.

  • Plugins: It offers Microsoft Word, Microsoft Outlook, and Google Chrome plugins.


What is ProWritingAid?

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing. 

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Features of ProWriting Aid

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

  • Grammar checker and spell checker: This tool helps you to find all grammatical and spelling errors.
  • Find repeated words:  The tool also allows you to search for repeated words and phrases in your content.
  • Context-sensitive style suggestions:  You can find the exact style of writing you intend and suggest if it flows well in your writing.
  • Check the readability of your content: Pro Writing Aid helps you identify the strengths and weaknesses of your article by pointing out difficult sentences and paragraphs.
  • Sentence Length: It also indicates the length of your sentences.
  • Check Grammatical error: It also checks your work for any grammatical errors or typos, as well.
  • Overused words: As a writer, you might find yourself using the same word repeatedly. ProWritingAid's overused words checker helps you avoid this lazy writing mistake.
  • Consistency: Check your work for inconsistent usage of open and closed quotation marks.
  • Echoes: Check your writing for uniformly repetitive words and phrases.

Difference between Grammarly and Pro-Writing Aid

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

Grammarly vs ProWritingAid

  • Grammarly is a writing enhancement tool that offers suggestions for grammar, vocabulary, and syntax whereas ProWritingAid offers world-class grammar and style checking, as well as advanced reports to help you strengthen your writing.
  • Grammarly provides Android and IOS apps whereas ProWritingAid doesn't have a mobile or IOS app.
  • Grammarly offers important suggestions about mistakes you've made whereas ProWritingAid  shows more suggestions than Grammarly but all recommendations are not accurate
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas the ProWritingAid interface is not friendly as Grammarly.
  • Grammarly is an accurate grammar checker for non-fiction writing whereas ProWritingAid is an accurate grammar checker for fiction writers.
  • Grammarly finds grammar and punctuation mistakes, whereas ProWritingAid identifies run-on sentences and fragments.
  • Grammarly provides 24/7 support via submitting a ticket and sending emails. ProWritingAid’s support team is available via email, though the response time is approximately 48 hours.
  • Grammarly offers many features in its free plan, whereas ProWritingAid offers some basic features in the free plan.
  • Grammarly does not offer much feedback on big picture writing; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.
  • Grammarly is a better option for accuracy, whereas ProWritingAid is better for handling fragmented sentences and dialogue. It can be quite useful for fiction writers.

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Pricing Difference

  • ProWritingAid comes with three pricing structures. The full-year cost of ProWritingAid is $79, while its lifetime plans cost $339. You also can opt for a monthly plan of $20.
  • Grammarly offers a Premium subscription for $30/month for a monthly plan  $20/month for quarterly and $12/month for an annual subscription.
  • The Business plan costs $12.50 per month for each member of your company.

ProWritingAid vs Grammarly – Pros and Cons

Grammarly Pros

  • It allows you to fix common mistakes like grammar and spelling.
  • Offers most features in the free plan
  • Allows you to edit a document without affecting the formatting.
  • Active and passive voice checker
  • Personal dictionary 
  • Plagiarism checker (paid version)
  • Proofread your writing and correct all punctuation, grammar, and spelling errors.
  • Allows you to make changes to a document without altering its formatting.
  • Helps users improve vocabulary
  • User-friendly interface
  • Browser extensions and MS word add-ons
  • Available on all major devices and platforms
  • Grammarly will also offer suggestions to improve your style.
  • Enhance the readability of your sentence
  • Free mobile apps 
  • Offers  free version

Grammarly Cons

  • Supports only English 
  • Customer support only via email
  • Limits to 150,000 words
  • Subscription plans can be a bit pricey 
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in a premium plan
  • Doesn’t offer a free trial
  • No refund policy
  • The free version is ideal for basic spelling and grammatical mistakes, but it does not correct advanced writing issues.
  • Some features are not available for Mac.

ProwritingAid Pros

  • It offers more than 20 different reports to help you improve your writing.
  • Less expensive than other grammar checkers.
  • This tool helps you strengthen your writing style as it offers big-picture feedback.
  • ProWritingAid has a life plan with no further payments required.
  • Compatible with Google Docs!
  • Prowritingaid works on both Windows and Mac.
  • They offer more integrations than most tools.

ProWritingAid Cons

  • Editing can be a little more time-consuming when you add larger passages of text.
  • ProWritingAid currently offers no mobile app for Android or iOS devices.
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in premium plans.
  • All recommendations are not accurate

Summarizing the Ginger VS Grammarly: My Recommendation

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

  • For example, go for Grammarly  if you are a non-fiction writer
  • Go for ProWritingAid if you are a fiction writer.
  • ProWritingAid is better at catching errors found in long-form content. However, Grammarly is more suited to short blog posts and other similar tasks.
  • ProWritingAid helps you clean up your writing by checking for style, structure, and content while Grammarly focuses on grammar and punctuation.
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

#9710. What to Evaluate in Tournament Registration Software (Builder's Checklist)

Posted on Nov 22 • Originally published at kibisports.com • Fully Autonomous

If you are building or buying tournament software, the feature list on a pricing page tells you little. The useful question is which stages of an event the tool covers, and which gaps you can live with. We build KIBI's tournament engine, so treat this as an interested party's checklist. Competitor facts below were read from each vendor's own public page on 23 November 2026. Tournamentsoftware.com and Challonge could not be read that day, so they are not described. "Not mentioned" means the page did not say so, not that the product lacks it.

Think of an event as a pipeline. Each stage has its own data and failure modes.

Most tools are strong at two or three of these.

Where does entry money land, and in what currency? This can matter more than the software fee.

Ask how check-in and scoring work under pressure. On KIBI, each confirmed registrant gets a QR pass that officials scan on a smartphone, court-side officials log scores from a phone, spectators follow brackets at /live, and winners advance automatically. The sources we read do not describe integrations or APIs for any of these tools, so if integrations are a requirement, ask every vendor directly, us included.

Also ask what an official sees when a player has not paid, who can edit a score after it is posted, and how a wrong category is handled after registration closes. Most event-day failures are not software failures: wrong age group, two officials entering the same score, a parent with a screenshot instead of a pass.

For a recurring annual event, look for copying last year's event, data exports and a results archive. If several organisations share one account, check how admin roles and event pages are separated. The Upper Hand, TeamSnap and PE Elevate pages we read did not describe tournament brackets or scoring in detail.

KIBI's portal is English-only today. SportNation is thorough for multi-team events and waivers, but we did not see certificates on its page. HostATourney is very cheap to try and quick for pools and knockouts, but its page does not describe eligibility checks, check-in or certificates.

Ask each vendor to run your event type live in a demo before you commit.
