#9708. Diagnosing Slow SQL Server Queries: A Practical Guide to Query Store and Execution Plans

Driving database innovation, optimizing data architecture, and scaling database performance to ensure reliability, security, and operational

Driving database innovation, optimizing data architecture, and scaling database performance to ensure reliability, security, and operational

Driving database innovation, optimizing data architecture, and scaling database performance to ensure reliability, security, and operational

Most slow-query investigations start in the wrong place: a CPU alert fires, someone opens the plan cache, and whatever is running right now gets tuned. That finds the loudest query, not necessarily the costliest one, and it says nothing about what changed.

Query Store supplies the missing piece: historical visibility. It records query text, execution plans, and runtime statistics over time intervals. Because this information is persisted in the user database, it survives SQL Server restarts. Execution plans then help explain why a particular query is slow.

This article covers a practical troubleshooting workflow for SQL Server 2016 and later:

Every example uses T-SQL. Replace the sample database names and identifiers with values from your own environment.

Query Store is available starting with SQL Server 2016. SQL Server 2022 enables it by default for newly created databases, but existing databases and upgraded environments should still be checked.

Next, configure its operating parameters:

For SQL Server 2017 and later, enable wait statistics capture separately:

These values are starting points, not universal production recommendations. Adjust the storage limit and retention period according to workload volume, query diversity, and monitoring requirements.

A useful habit is to verify Query Store's state periodically:

If actual_state_desc differs from desired_state_desc, investigate why Query Store is not operating as expected.

Start with one question: Which queries consumed the most resources over the last 24 hours?

Query A looks worse when examining individual execution time. However, Query B may consume considerably more cumulative resources.

Query Store records average runtime statistics and execution counts for individual intervals. Multiplying the averages by execution counts provides an estimate of cumulative consumption.

The following query identifies the top 10 queries by total execution duration:

A few details matter when interpreting these results:

The time filter uses interval boundaries, so it can include executions from an interval that began before the exact 24-hour cutoff. The results are therefore an interval-based approximation rather than an exact rolling 24-hour measurement.

Run the query three times, changing the final ordering:

Queries appearing in multiple lists deserve closer investigation.

The SSMS Top Resource Consuming Queries report provides a graphical view of similar information. However, keeping a reusable SQL script makes it easier to automate reporting and compare workload trends over time.

A query that suddenly becomes slower without an application code change often deserves a plan investigation.

Query Store allows you to compare execution plans associated with the same query. First, identify the relevant query_id from the previous step. Then examine its historical plans.

This query calculates execution-count-weighted average duration and logical reads for each plan over the selected interval window.

These numbers are illustrative, but they show the kind of regression worth investigating.

Plan 23 takes considerably longer and performs significantly more logical reads.

The next step is to establish when the change occurred and correlate it with:

SQL Server Management Studio also provides the Regressed Queries report, which helps visualize performance changes and compare execution plans side by side. An important distinction: a different plan is not automatically a bad plan. The objective is to identify whether the plan change explains the observed performance degradation.

Query Store preserves compiled execution plans, but these plans generally contain estimated row counts rather than actual runtime row counts. For actual execution information, capture an actual execution plan by rerunning the query with Include Actual Execution Plan enabled in SSMS.

On SQL Server 2019 and later, you can also enable last-query-plan statistics:

The sys.dm_exec_query_plan_stats function can then provide the last known actual execution plan for a cached plan handle.

Remember that this is last-execution information, not a complete historical collection of actual execution plans.

When examining an execution plan, I recommend following this order.

One of the most useful indicators is the difference between estimated and actual row counts.

The optimizer expected approximately 100 rows but encountered 12,000.

That difference can influence downstream decisions, including join selection, memory grants, and parallelism.

A significant estimation difference is a diagnostic clue, not automatic proof that statistics are the problem.

Parameter sniffing occurs when SQL Server compiles a parameterized query using particular parameter values and reuses the resulting execution plan for subsequent executions. This can become problematic when parameter values have highly different data distributions.

For example, consider an orders table where:

An execution plan optimized for the second customer may perform poorly when reused for the first. In an actual execution plan, inspect the parameter information, including:

A significant difference between these values, combined with skewed data and inconsistent performance, can indicate parameter sensitivity.

An Index Seek is not always better than an Index Scan. SQL Server chooses an access method based on estimated cost, cardinality, available indexes, and the amount of data required. However, certain patterns deserve investigation.

Before creating an index, evaluate existing indexes, write overhead, storage consumption, and whether the proposed index would actually improve the workload.

For example, comparing an integer column with a string parameter can introduce an implicit conversion and prevent an efficient index access path in some circumstances. Similarly, spills to tempdb can indicate that an operator received an insufficient memory grant. These warnings help identify where further investigation is needed.

SQL Server may suggest missing indexes in execution plans. However, these suggestions do not understand the entire indexing strategy of your application.

Before creating a suggested index, consider:

The goal is not to maximize the number of indexes. It is to improve the overall workload.

Once you understand the problem, address the underlying cause. A reasonable troubleshooting order is:

Sometimes the root cause cannot be fixed immediately. For example, a vendor application may generate SQL that cannot be modified without a lengthy release process. SQL Server 2022 introduced Query Store hints, which allow administrators to apply supported query hints without changing application code.

This applies a recompilation hint to the selected Query Store query.

It is important to understand that OPTION (RECOMPILE) is not plan forcing. It instructs SQL Server to compile a new plan for each execution, which can help with parameter-sensitive workloads but also introduces compilation overhead.

Another option is to force a previously successful execution plan.

This tells SQL Server to use the selected historical plan when possible. Plan forcing should be treated as a temporary mitigation rather than a permanent solution. A forced plan may become less efficient as data distributions and workloads change. It may also fail to apply if required database objects or indexes are no longer available.

Since SQL Server 2017, automatic plan correction is also available on supported SQL Server configurations.

Check edition and platform support before enabling automatic tuning.

Even when automatic correction is available, monitor its decisions and validate that the forced plans continue to perform well.

Consider an e-commerce application where the order history endpoint starts responding slowly. Initially, the endpoint responds in approximately 200 milliseconds. After a deployment and a change in workload distribution, response times increase to several seconds. The development team initially suspects application code. However, Query Store reveals something different.

Investigation 1: Identify the expensive query

The query appears near the top of the total-duration report. Its execution count has increased, and its average duration is substantially higher than its historical baseline.

Query Store shows that the query has two historical plans. The newer plan performs significantly more logical reads.

Investigation 3: Inspect the actual execution plan

The team finds that a parameter-sensitive query is using an inefficient plan for customers with large order histories. The actual row counts differ significantly from the estimates.

The team evaluates the available indexes, reviews statistics, and tests a suitable parameter-sensitive query optimization. If an immediate application change is not possible, a Query Store hint or a previously successful plan may provide a temporary mitigation.

The objective is not simply to make one execution faster. It is to restore predictable performance across the workload.

Even with Query Store enabled, several issues can affect the accuracy of your investigation.

1. Query Store stops collecting information

A full Query Store can transition into read-only mode.

Check sys.database_query_store_options regularly, especially actual_state_desc, desired_state_desc, and readonly_reason.

2. Ad hoc workloads inflate storage consumption

Applications that generate many unparameterized queries can create large numbers of distinct query entries. Use an appropriate capture mode and investigate parameterization opportunities.

A reasonable average duration can hide occasional executions that take several seconds. Examine maximum duration, standard deviation, execution counts, and individual runtime intervals before deciding that a plan is healthy.

4. Time zones create misleading correlations

Query Store timestamps are stored in UTC. Convert timestamps appropriately before comparing them with application logs, deployment records, or monitoring dashboards.

5. Historical statistics are not necessarily actual execution plans

Query Store provides valuable plan history and aggregated runtime statistics, but it should not be mistaken for a complete historical record of actual execution plans with actual row counts. Use actual execution plans and appropriate runtime diagnostics when deeper investigation is necessary.

The examples in this article target different SQL Server versions.

Always verify the feature's availability and configuration requirements for your SQL Server edition and deployment environment.

Diagnosing slow SQL queries requires more than identifying expensive operators in an execution plan. The most effective approach combines historical workload information with detailed execution-plan analysis.

The tooling is not the hardest part of SQL Server performance troubleshooting. What separates a ten-minute diagnosis from a three-day investigation is having the historical evidence to understand what changed. Query Store provides that evidence. Execution plans help explain it. Together, they give database engineers a repeatable approach to diagnosing and resolving SQL Server performance problems.

#9705. A Payment Webhook Should Not Grant the Same Purchase Twice

When a learning platform sells a digital resource, the interesting part of payment integration is often the second notification.

The first confirmed payment can grant access. A repeated notification must not grant it again, record another collection, or create a second purchase event for advertising analytics.

I am Hassan Essam, founder of Snuhy, an Egyptian learning and digital services platform. This is a small design note about a rule we use when defining payment behavior: count a sale after confirmed payment, and preserve one identity for that sale across retries.

The example below is explanatory pseudocode, not an extract from our production code or a complete payment integration.

An integration can have at least three identifiers:

Deduplicating only the event ID is insufficient if two distinct notifications describe the same payment. Deduplicating only the order ID can also be wrong when an order legitimately supports multiple collections.

Choose the business key for the action. An access grant might be unique per order and product. A collection should use the confirmed payment identity. An advertising purchase event needs the identity of the sale it represents.

A unique constraint is part of correctness here. Two workers can both pass an application-level “does this exist?” check before either inserts a record. The database needs to reject the conflicting duplicate.

The exact keys and transitions depend on the payment provider and business model. An installment collection, a full purchase, and a refund should not be forced into one event merely because all three involve money.

An outbox helps avoid a committed payment with a missing notification job. It does not eliminate the uncertainty of an external request.

A provider might accept a request just before the worker loses its connection. Retrying without reconciliation can duplicate the external effect. Use the destination's supported idempotency or event-deduplication mechanism, retain the result, and distinguish known failure from uncertain acceptance.

For purchase measurement, use a stable sale identity. If browser and server both report the same sale, configure the destination's deduplication mechanism consistently. Also check measurement consent before enqueueing or sending; confirmation of payment is not itself marketing consent.

These checks should use isolated fixtures, fake external services, and test-provider facilities. There is no need to create fake revenue in a live financial ledger to prove that retries are handled.

The customer-facing consequence is straightforward: a repeated technical notification should not look like a second purchase. Achieving that requires each downstream action to have a defined business identity and an explicit retry policy.

Disclosure: I am the founder of Snuhy. This article was drafted with AI assistance from recorded project requirements and is presented as a conceptual design example. It makes no claim of a measured conversion uplift or a provider-certified implementation.

#9703. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9701. A free OpenAPI diff that never uploads your spec

Posted on Nov 22 • Originally published at graphwake.com

Pasting an internal API spec into a website is a hard sell. The spec lists every endpoint and every field, and sometimes the hosts behind them, so you want to know where it goes.

We build Graphwake, which tells the teams that consume an API when a change in its OpenAPI spec is about to break them. Along the way we built a free OpenAPI diff where the comparison runs in your browser tab. Paste the old and the new spec, choose two files or give two URLs, and it shows every change that can break a client. Free, no sign-up.

A breaking change is one that can make an existing client fail. These come first in every result:

A new optional field, endpoint or response code breaks no one. Those are listed separately, out of your way.

The "Try an example" result: 3 breaking changes, each under the line it comes from.

A file you choose is read in the tab. A URL is fetched by your browser straight from that address, so that server has to allow it (CORS). We never receive the spec, the file or the URL. If you want to check, keep the Network tab of your DevTools open while you compare.

Two limits come with running in the browser. A spec can be up to 10 MB of text, but very large specs, a few megabytes of YAML, can take longer than the 20 seconds the browser check allows; the result then says so. And references to other files ($ref: ./schemas.yaml) can't be followed, so bundle the spec into one file first.

A diff tells you what changed. Whether the change is safe depends on something else: who calls this endpoint? The author of the change usually doesn't know, and nobody keeps the list.

Example: the same kind of breaking change, sent only to the teams that call the endpoint.

Do you paste internal specs into online tools today, or is that off limits where you work?

About Graphwake. We build Graphwake, a dependency map for your APIs. It watches your OpenAPI specs, knows which teams consume each endpoint, and tells only those teams in Slack, Microsoft Teams or email when a change is about to break them. Start a 7-day free trial at graphwake.com

#9697. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

#9695. Why I Chose Node.js Storage for Generated Images and Temporary Download Links

When an e-commerce app stores AI-generated images, the hard part is not writing bytes. It is moving large files to the right tenant without turning every download into an application-server transfer. Short answer: store private objects in object storage and mint a short-lived signed URL only when a user requests an export. That keeps the delivery path fast and leaves the vendor choice reversible.

For this exact workflow, Infrai is a reasonable first candidate when one REST credential should cover storage and the rest of a backend. The useful test is still throughput and replaceability, not a logo.

I care about time-to-first-call and the amount of glue a CLI needs. My first sketch put image data in a database and streamed it through Node.js. That was a bad boundary: exports competed with API traffic, and a retry could repeat a large upload. The useful boundary is an object key such as tenant_42/jobs/job_8f2/result.webp; the database owns who can see it, while storage owns the bytes.

Give each generated image a record containing user_id, prompt_id or job id, object key, MIME type, and size. That index is more dependable than trying to search object metadata. Before showing a download action, an object-head call can confirm that the key exists and report its current size. For a tenant export, authorize the user against the database record first, then create a URL with an expiry that matches the workflow.

Here is the small TypeScript client I use for the two calls in that path. It makes the HTTP method explicit, keeps the key out of source control, and backs off on rate limits. The presign operation is a request, not a public ACL; the resulting link is temporary.

The exact response envelope is part of the provider contract, so production code should validate payload.url before returning it. I would also make the database lookup the authorization gate; possession of an object key must never be treated as tenant access.

Large-file throughput shifts the bottleneck to upload and copy strategy. Keep the API server out of the data path where possible: have the worker write directly to the object store, then persist the metadata row. If a single image must appear under two prefixes (for example, a tenant folder and an audit export), use object copy rather than downloading and re-uploading the same bytes through Node.js. That is less glue and fewer opportunities to corrupt a transfer.

For a bursty catalog job, I would queue generation and export records, cap concurrent downloads per tenant, and measure object size before creating links. The queue should carry the tenant id, job id, key, MIME type, and expected size; workers can reject a stale record before touching storage, while a per-tenant semaphore prevents one catalog refresh from consuming every connection. My benchmark counters are boring on purpose: bytes written, presign latency, head latency, and completed links. A pretty dashboard cannot tell me whether a 200 MB export is starving checkout traffic.

S3-compatible APIs make the application boundary portable, but compatibility is not identical feature coverage. Here is the decision table I keep beside the migration checklist.

Infrai is worth trying when you want the storage workflow behind plain HTTP and already use other backend capabilities under the same credential. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples reduce SDK glue, and the storage contract is small enough to wrap behind an interface. That is the concrete portability play: my Node.js code depends on put, head, copy, and presign semantics, not on a vendor-specific object model.

The catch is real. Infrai has no public-read ACL, so it is not suitable for a permanent public image CDN or a static website that expects anonymous URLs. It also lacks object versioning and object lock; an accidental overwrite is not recoverable through those features. There is no If-Match conditional write, no automatic cross-region replication, and no cross-cloud bulk migration tool. Browser direct uploads need a CORS setup that the service does not expose as an independent route. Stick with S3 when you need those controls, or choose a specialist such as R2 when edge delivery is the primary concern.

Lifecycle rules have a one-day minimum, and multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule. Metadata is not server-searchable; list operations filter by prefix. Those are design constraints, not surprises to hide in a postmortem. Put retention and concurrency policy in your queue and database, and document a separate disaster-recovery copy if the product needs one.

Define a storage adapter whose public methods accept a tenant id and return an object key or signed URL. Store that key in your database, never in a URL column. During a provider move, copy objects, switch the adapter, and keep old links short-lived so the cutover window stays bounded. A copy route is useful here, but replication is still your responsibility.

I am not sure any single storage vendor wins every export workload; your mileage may vary with region, object size, and queue limits. The stable choice is the one you can replace without rewriting authorization and job tracking. For private AI images, that means object storage plus on-demand signed links, with throughput measured at the object boundary.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage contract and discovery examples at https://docs.infrai.cc.

#9694. How long can butter sit out?: For the best baking success, here's the deal on saving softened butter for later.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions.

Ryan from our Baker’s Hotline is here with the answer.

You sure can! It will still work the next time you want to bake. But remember, as with any dairy product, there are always precautions to take.

The USDA recommends keeping butter at room temperature for no more than two days to prevent spoilage. Salt is a preservative and can lengthen the shelf life, but for the sake of this article, we’re talking about unsalted butter. (It’s more appropriate for baking and is the type called for in most King Arthur recipes.)

“If the butter has only been on the counter at room temperature for a few hours or overnight and has maintained a temperature below 70°F, it should be just fine to place back in the fridge,” says Ryan. “You may not notice a difference in the performance of the butter when you eventually use it, other than the wrapper being a bit wet or soft. Food safety-wise, it’s still good to use.”

“If the butter became very soft or started to melt during its time on the counter (or in the microwave if you were speeding up the process), you can put it back in the fridge, but it may not be the best to use in your recipe,” Ryan suggests. “You may notice when it solidifies that it’s separated or grainy. The water, fats, and solids in butter are an emulsion, which can break when melted and re-solidified.” If your recipe depends on butter to create air or structure, like a cake that calls for creaming butter and sugar, you’ll want to start over with new butter.

“If you used that butter in a recipe requiring creaming, the air you incorporate wouldn’t be as stable since the structure of the butter has changed,” Ryan says. “Your baked goods may not rise properly, and frostings may be soft and loose. Is it still safe to use? Food safety-wise, yes. But structure-wise, perhaps not.”

That butter can still be used for other things though! Extra-softened or even melted and re-solidified butter will still work perfectly to spread on toast or pancakes, to be made into brown butter, or to remelt and use in recipes calling for melted butter like a Graham Cracker Crust.

If your butter has been unrefrigerated for more than two days, you run the risk of it going rancid. As Ryan says, “There is no coming back from rancid butter.” It has a distinctly unpleasant flavor and a noticeable rancid smell that carries over into baked goods. It’s best to dispose of the butter if this happens.

But what if you want to keep your butter at room temperature for days at a time to slather on your morning toast? Ryan recommends storing your butter in a butter keeper if you want to leave it on the counter. “The water in the base of the jar creates an airtight seal, helping prevent the butter from spoiling. So long as it is stored away from direct heat and light, the butter in a container like this will be fine for a few days. Be sure to replace the water often and clean the container before filling again.”

“When working with butter in a recipe, I like to bring out and soften only the amount that is needed for what I am working on. That way, I don’t end up with extra butter that won’t be used right away,” he says. “Repeatedly moving butter from the fridge to the counter and then back invites spoilage and poor performance.”

In a rush? To soften your butter more quickly, Ryan advises, “Cut your butter into pats and place them on a plate in a single layer at room temperature. More surface area means that the butter will soften a bit faster!”

#9691. What is piloncillo? This sweetener makes great cookies, pan dulce, and more: Use this traditional Mexican unrefined sugar for a dash of flavor and history.

This article is part of our feature celebrating Pan Dulce. Find all things pan dulce here.

Categorically, piloncillo is a “non-centrifugal” cane sugar, meaning it is an unrefined sugar product and a true natural brown sugar. It’s mostly consumed in Mexico and Latin America, but a similar product can be found in Asia, known as jaggery in India. Though often lumped together, these unrefined dark sugars are very different from brown sugars on the market today, which have been refined to a large degree — in some cases, they’re actually just white sugar with coloring or molasses added.

Making piloncillo, on the other hand, involves an artisanal process that’s hundreds of years old. To make it, pressed cane juice is boiled to evaporate the water and deeply caramelize the sugar. The cooked cane is then poured into molds (often made of wood) and left to dry and harden. Traditional piloncillo is conical in shape and can vary in size from small to large cones but is most commonly found in a medium size that weighs about 200 grams. In Guatemala and Colombia, it is called panela, where it is cooked to a lighter degree and typically formed into a brick, rather than cone, shape. Other forms of piloncillo can be granulated or liquid (which is more rare).

Minimally processed and boldly flavored, piloncillo was historically a prized and respected foodstuff. As an unrefined cane sugar, piloncillo provides more complex vitamins and minerals than refined sugars, which undergo processing and whitening methods that also strip nutrients from the whole food. And piloncillo is also great for baking, providing notes of burnt caramel and hints of smoke. Plus, its rich molasses qualities keep baked goods moist and fresh for longer.

Always look at the ingredient label when purchasing piloncillo and make sure it says 100% pure cane juice or cane sugar. It is becoming increasingly common to find imitation products marketed as jaggery or piloncillo that contain coloring and corn syrup. You can find good piloncillo at specialty grocery stores or online at retailers.

In Mexico and throughout Latin America, piloncillo is an important ingredient in many traditional dishes. (Some will even say it’s not the “real dish” if you substitute sugar in these recipes due to the deep flavors and richness that only piloncillo can provide.) This deep, dark unrefined sugar lends its characteristic flavor and texture to popular foods and beverages such as capirotada, tepache, coyotas, atole, café de olla, calabaza al horno, coricos, and hojarascas, to name a few!

I love adding piloncillo when I’m making champurrado. In this warm and thick chocolate beverage, the piloncillo is chopped or grated and dissolved in the pot with water or milk before adding the chocolate and masa. In this recipe, the piloncillo’s intense sweet and smoky flavors pair well with the chocolate and corn masa.

While there are many dishes and uses for piloncillo, it’s not a simple substitution for granulated white sugar in recipes, but you can use it the same as you would brown sugar with a 1:1 substitution by weight.  Depending on how hard the cone is, it can be crumbled or grated for easier measuring. If it is very hard, try cutting it in half with a sharp knife and then placing it between parchment paper or a towel and beating with a rolling pin.

Find puerquitos and many more Mexican sweets in our feature celebrating pan dulce.

#9687. Upgrade Your Next Grilled Cheese With A Rich & Creamy Store-Bought Spread

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

The essence of the best grilled cheese lies in the delicious combination of melted cheese and crisped bread. There are many methods to accomplish such a pairing, with plenty of tips to give you the best results imaginable. If you're after a version that's especially ooey-gooey, try making the sandwich with cheddar cheese spread.

Available from several brands at widespread grocery stores like Walmart, cheddar cheese spread is essentially cheddar mixed with butter. The foodstuff is easily spreadable on bread and melts when it's heated, making a grilled cheese with a pleasantly runny interior. While it's creamier than classic cheddar, the flavor is no afterthought, with this cheese's sharpness still perceptible.

Using butter alongside cheese is common in grilled cheese recipes; the spread lets you conveniently lather on both components at once. The fat enhances the bread's crispiness, all while retaining a moist interior. As a sole filling, the spread turns the dish luxuriously decadent — but complemented with a few slices of cheese, it's a grilled cheese rendition to remember.

There are many international grilled cheese styles to explore; cheddar cheese spread fits into a wide range of renditions. Combined with a store-bought loaf of sourdough and sliced cheddar, the spread makes a mouth-watering classic. However, you can consider layering in other ingredients, too — thereby making a cheddar grilled cheese with a twist.

For example, the cheese's sharpness welcomes a sweet contrast. Spread a jam or jelly into the sandwich, whether a rich fig jam, tart cranberry preserves, or a sweet blackberry jam. For a sweet touch with less sugar, you could also use fresh fruits to upgrade any grilled cheese; the spread would go great with apples, for example, as apples and cheddar are a match made in sandwich heaven. And you could also consider leaning into the spice, smearing on spicy brown mustard or hot pepper jelly for a light dose of heat.

Consider trying out other ingredient add-ins, too. Caramelized onions will lend a grilled cheese a subtle nutty sweetness, while bacon bits bring a savory touch. Cheddar cheese spreads allow the many different flavors to come together, letting you easily craft a sandwich to your tastes.

#9686. 16 pumpkin recipes, from cakes and cookies to bars and bread: We've got a marbled pumpkin cake, chewy pumpkin cookies, and even pumpkin milk bread.

It’s that time of year when pumpkin spice everything starts appearing on store shelves — candles, lip balm, air fresheners, beer, and of course, the ubiquitous PSL (pumpkin spice latte). That means fall is here, and more importantly, that pumpkin should make a grand return to your kitchen! Pull out your canned pumpkin — or better yet, make your own pumpkin purée — and stock your pantry with pumpkin pie spice, because we have the best pumpkin recipes to bake this fall.

This Pumpkin Swirl Cake takes my breath away every time I unmold it from its intricate loaf pan. The anticipation keeps building until I slice into the pound cake-like loaf and reveal the swirled pattern inside, marbled with both vanilla and spiced pumpkin batter. (Don’t fret if you don’t have the specialty loaf pan — this can also be baked in a standard loaf pan and adorned with a simple confectioners’ sugar icing.)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Patch O Pumpkins Loaf Pan and Pure Vanilla Plus

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Sparkling Sugar

A cousin of Belgian-style Liège waffles, these Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles have caramelized edges and a pleasant chew that’s reminiscent of brioche. The yeasted batter has pumpkin in it for flavor and color, plus Swedish pearl sugar that melts into pockets of crispy sugar. The best part? The batter rests overnight, so if you prepare it the night ahead, all you have to do the next morning is scoop and cook the batter for hot, crispy waffles in just a few minutes.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles

To make this recipe, you'll need: Swedish Pearl Sugar

I used to make the same pumpkin pie recipe for years, and it always left me wanting a little more excitement. Then I found this Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie and never looked back! The generously spiced filling uses nutmeg, ginger, cloves, and Vietnamese cinnamon to create a more flavorful pie than traditional versions. The secret to its silky-smooth texture? Corn syrup, which is an invert sugar and keeps the custard from becoming grainy. Substitute another invert sugar like honey or maple syrup if you like; I use maple syrup.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon, Ginger, and Nutmeg

Whenever I have these tender, golden scones on hand, I look forward to getting out of bed the next morning because I know they’re waiting for me. They can be easily customized to use a range of mix-ins, depending on what you have in your pantry. My personal preference is a mix of crystallized ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits.

Get the recipe: Harvest Pumpkin Scones (or Gluten-Free Pumpkin Scones)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Mini Diced Ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits

If you’re looking for a way to make your whole kitchen smell like fall, these one-bowl, easy pumpkin muffins deliver — and fast. They’re ready in under an hour, so you can spend less time measuring, mixing, and cleaning and more time tackling your autumn bucket list.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Standard Muffin Pan

Making banana bread is an almost weekly activity in my house — except during fall, when we pivot to pumpkin bread instead. This is a quick, easy bake that satisfies my craving for something pumpkin-y, and it uses a simple trick to concentrate the pumpkin flavor and ensure the loaf is perfectly textured: The pumpkin purée is reduced on the stovetop to cook off excess moisture. (The process is similar to browning butter.) As a result, the final loaf is packed with pumpkin flavor.

Get the recipe: The Most Pumpkin Pumpkin Chocolate Chip Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: Ginger and Semisweet Chocolate Chips

These bars have all the cozy, spiced goodness of the classic dessert in a portable, crowd-friendly form. The buttery, brown sugar crust gets pressed into the pan (no rolling out pie dough!), and the silky pumpkin filling comes together with just a handful of ingredients. The (optional but highly recommended) sour cream whipped topping brings a slight tanginess and completes the traditional pumpkin pie experience.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Milk Bread is exceptionally soft, squishy, and feather-light, while also packing in a lot of pumpkin. Pumpkin can often weigh down baked goods, but here the combination of a tangzhong, bread flour, and a long mix makes this bread simultaneously moist and high-rising.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant Yeast

This tender pumpkin crumb cake is for people who double the chocolate chips in pumpkin bread and the streusel on coffee cake. Atop the thin layer of spiced pumpkin cake lays a heavy blanket of buttery crumbs with a bold chocolate flavor, thanks to Dutch-processed cocoa powder.

Get the recipe: Chocolate-Pumpkin Crumb Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Black Cocoa

These Pumpkin Cupcakes, with their piped swirl of cream cheese frosting, are the ideal way to celebrate fall birthdays. The cupcakes are super tender, thanks to the addition of cake flour and oil. It has two layers of espresso swirl tucked within a moist, spiced cake. Make it in your favorite Bundt pan or serve it as a loaf if you’re more of simple-is-better person. #9684. 22 Recipes To Make With Thanksgiving Leftovers

Turkey, ham, mashed potatoes, casseroles, pumpkin, cranberries, stuffing ... the annual fall-flavored feast that we know and love is always a crowd-pleasing holiday meal to look forward to. And one of the best things about Thanksgiving isn't just the meal itself; it's all of the delicious leftovers that inevitably follow.

Especially when you're hosting a crowd (which is possible to do stress-free with these tips from Guy Fieri), those leftovers can be abundant. But the beauty is that there's so much more you can do with your Thanksgiving leftovers than just reheat and re-eat. From soups, sandwiches, and snacks that repurpose your ingredients to completely new dishes that transform the original elements of the meal, you can take those leftovers in so many directions.

If you're looking for new ideas or creative ways to use up what's left in the fridge, we've got a plethora of recipes to try that'll help you make the most of your Thanksgiving leftovers. (Pro tip: Just don't forget the 2-2-2 rule with your leftovers to ensure food safety.)

Whether you enjoyed some mac & cheese on Thanksgiving Day or not, this recipe is a whole new twist on the classic that infuses the beloved dish with holiday flavor. It's honestly a little shocking how many leftover ingredients manage to make their way into this one recipe, but when you think about it ... how could it not taste good?

This Thanksgiving Leftover Macaroni & Cheese incorporates three different types of cheese — fontina, cheddar, and mascarpone — to make the cheese sauce. Then come the Thanksgiving leftovers that get folded into the dish: shredded turkey meat, sweet potatoes, peas, and pasta. After it's baked, the whole thing is topped off with some cranberry sauce to bring the Thanksgiving flavors home.

Recipe: Thanksgiving Leftover Macaroni & Cheese

Now, this is a fun one — it's Thanksgiving dinner in burger form! Not only can you use that leftover stuffing, but this recipe also calls for turkey meat, gravy, and cranberry sauce, so this one wins for maximizing whatever's taking up space in the fridge. And it's incredibly tasty, too.

The "burger" is a combination of stuffing, turkey, eggs, and milk in patty form. The patty is then griddled in some butter and topped off with cranberry sauce, gravy, and goat cheese to create a burger that'll leave you stuffed in the best way.

Recipe: Leftover Thanksgiving Stuffing Burger

Okay, a turkey cheesesteak might seem a little contradictory, but this one's worth entertaining when it comes to making the most of your Thanksgiving leftovers. You won't just knock out the leftover turkey, but also any leftover gravy with this Thanksgiving Leftover Turkey Cheesesteak.

The cheesesteak starts with sautéed sweet onions, and then the turkey (dark meat works great if you have it), gravy, and cornichons are added to the mix before two types of cheese (provolone and American cheese) are melted on top. Everything is stuffed into toasty hoagie rolls to make a saucy, messy, tasty Thanksgiving cheesesteak.

Recipe: Thanksgiving Leftover Turkey Cheesesteak

Why not whip up the ultimate comfort meal to enjoy the weekend after Thanksgiving? Once the holiday winds down, you can use your leftover turkey (and any extra pumpkin puree you might have lying around) in this Pumpkin and Turkey Chili recipe. This fall take on a classic slow cooker chili recipe incorporates pumpkin puree into the stew along with a blend of warm spices like cinnamon, cloves, and nutmeg.

To sub in your already-cooked turkey, just skip the initial step where you'd brown the ground turkey, and instead add some cubed or shredded turkey once your chili is simmering.

Making croquettes is a fun and delicious way to use up that leftover turkey. Croquettes actually originated in France as a way to use up leftover meats and vegetables, so they're the perfect way to repurpose those Thanksgiving leftovers.

The cheesy croquettes are made by sautéeing mushrooms, onions, and garlic and combining the mixture with cooked turkey, parsley, and mozzarella cheese. They're then shaped into balls, dipped into egg and breadcrumbs, and lightly fried until golden brown and crispy.

Recipe: Crispy Turkey and Cheese Croquettes

Shepherd's pie is a great follow-up recipe to Thanksgiving if you need a way to reuse copious amounts of mashed potatoes, because that iconic mashed potato topping makes shepherd's pie what it is. This particular recipe is made with ground lamb and vegetables like corn, peas, and carrots as the base of the pie, but you could easily sub in your leftover turkey as well if you want to knock out two leftovers in one go.

Either way, this Simple Shepherd's Pie is even easier to make since the mashed potatoes are already done. All you need to do is assemble, bake, and enjoy ... or if you're feeling ambitious, you can try one of these 15 secret ingredients to make your Shepherd's Pie the best it can be.

Bought too many potatoes on your Thanksgiving grocery run? This casserole will come in handy for those extra ingredients. The simple, easy-to-make dish combines potatoes, onions, bacon, and thyme with cream, chicken stock, and cheese. Everything gets baked until it's melty and delicious, making a perfect side dish to pair with any leftover meat from the holiday.

This recipe uses blue cheese, which complements the bacon, but you can feel free to use any cheese you like (cheddar, mozzarella, or even Gruyère would all work great).

This comforting soup brings together many ingredients that were most likely on your Thanksgiving shopping list, including carrots, apples, potatoes, and pecans. It's the perfect meal to throw together that'll make use of all of those extra groceries that you're not sure what to do with. Carrots and apples may not be your first thoughts as the base of a soup, but trust us, this comforting soup recipe is a (somewhat unexpected) winner.

All you need to do is cook your vegetables down with plenty of flavorful herbs and spices like cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, and fresh thyme. Add your stock, blend until smooth, and finish off with the cream for a nutty and rich yet soothing soup that you can work your way through all week.

For all those who may have purchased some fresh pumpkins for your Thanksgiving pie but didn't get around to using all of it, we've got just the recipe. As a bonus, it'll use up those extra potatoes, too!

Put a fall spin on a classic potato gratin by slicing your pumpkin into pieces or rounds the same size as your potatoes. The cream mixture, which is made up of heavy cream, garlic, thyme, rosemary, and salt, gets layered with your pumpkin and potatoes; then everything is covered with grated Swiss cheese and baked longer than you may think until the whole dish is bubbly, browned, and cheesy.

Whether you've got some extra sweet potatoes lying around from a casserole side dish or a sweet potato pie, this Sweet Potato Tarte Tatin is a delicious way to use them up. And with a little puff pastry, this dish looks impressive but doesn't take long to make a classic tarte tatin.

The trick is making the caramel element; once you've gotten that down, the rest is smooth sailing. Your homemade caramel will come together with sliced sweet potatoes and a puff pastry covering to produce an irresistible starchy take on the tarte tatin.

Similar to the tarte tatin, you can use a store-bought dough (this time, paper-thin Greek phyllo pastry) to keep this dessert simple. Baklava is typically made with nuts, but this recipe replaces that crunchy ingredient with a smooth pumpkin puree — along with spices like cinnamon, nutmeg, and clove — for a tasty fall twist on this decadent, flaky treat.

Baklava involves making a simple syrup of sorts, and then it's all about layering (and this hack for assembling can make your baklava process even quicker). In the end, you'll have an extremely crispy, sweet-yet-spiced dessert born from leftover pumpkin puree.

If there's one thing you may not have thought to do with your leftover pumpkin and cranberries, it might be homemade liqueur. It might seem a little extreme, but it's not as complicated as it sounds, and you will be rewarded with an ingredient that'll help level up your baking and cocktails for many weeks to come.

In short, the process just involves cooking down your chosen ingredient with sugar, then adding a high-proof liquor like vodka, and then straining it and letting it sit. That's it!

Recipe: Cranberry Liqueur and Pumpkin Liqueur

If you didn't quite make as much apple pie filling as you planned, don't worry — this one's for you. It's basically a shortcut apple pie filling that you can throw on some ice cream, douse in whipped cream, or simply enjoy on its own.

This Sweet Spiced Baked Apples recipe is one of the easiest ways to make use of all of those leftover apples. Any apples will do: Honeycrisp, Fuji, Pink Lady, you name it. All you need to do is bake them with an undeniably delicious mixture of brown sugar, walnuts, butter, and spices. It's so simple, and so satisfying.

Sticking with those leftover apples, this recipe will make a fantastic breakfast or brunch in the days following Thanksgiving. The Americanized origins of Dutch baby pancakes are a bit complicated, but long story short, this creation is essentially a giant, skillet-baked pancake. And it's a great go-to dish to capitalize on your extra apples, because you most likely have everything else you need stocked in your kitchen.

This Dutch baby recipe uses a batter made of flour, milk, eggs, honey, vanilla extract, salt, and melted butter. Next, pour the batter over thinly sliced apples that have been tossed in brown sugar and cinnamon. Everything is then baked together to perfection until your leftover apples turn into puffy, golden goodness.

This is a unique and flavorful way to use any extra pumpkins you have from the holiday. The bonus? The presentation is impressive, so if you find yourself continuing to host through the weekend, this is another great meal to provide for your guests that will help you repurpose some of your Thanksgiving ingredients.

With everything from coconut milk and ground pork to ginger, soy sauce, and water chestnuts, this rice dish includes a lot of really interesting ingredients that may not seem like they belong together, but they all unite to build a warm, aromatic meal. Just trust the process, serve it up inside a pumpkin, and watch your guests marvel.

Recipe: Stuffed Pumpkin With Aromatic Rice

Although this recipe includes a lot of similar ingredients as the above (rice, pumpkin, nuts), the elements come together in a totally different way to create a totally different dish: a warmly spiced, sweet rice pudding that'll taste just like your Thanksgiving pumpkin pie.

The dessert is made with Arborio rice, almond milk, maple syrup, pumpkin puree, vanilla, and spices — everything gets simmered together until it thickens into a pudding, then chilled and served with glazed pecans for extra crunch.

Leftovers truly shine when you use them to build a great sandwich. Meet this Sweet and Savory Monte Cristo Sandwich, which can be made with your leftover Thanksgiving turkey and ham. In addition to the sliced duo of meat, this sandwich features Gruyère cheese, mayo, and raspberry jam (although you can obviously sub in some cranberry sauce if you so please), all stacked between slices of brioche bread.

What makes this Monte Cristo extra delicious is the French toast treatment that it gets: Once assembled, the entire sandwich is dipped in a mixture of egg, half-and-half, and nutmeg and lightly fried in butter until golden brown. Oh, it's then topped off with some powdered sugar for good measure.

Recipe: Sweet And Savory Monte Cristo Sandwich

Here's another fun breakfast recipe to keep things interesting over the holiday weekend! This take on a Croque Madame (a classic French sandwich typically made with ham, cheese, and Mornay sauce and topped with a sunny-side-up egg) creates a "waffled" version of the sandwich by employing a waffle iron as the cooking tool.

Where do the leftovers come in? The waffle "batter" is made with your leftover Thanksgiving stuffing, which you'll then combine with milk and eggs. This concoction is then topped with slices of ham and grated cheddar cheese, and finished off with a fried or poached egg. Post-Thanksgiving brunch is served.

If you've still got some sweet potatoes left from your holiday shopping, this is another great recipe to make use of them — and it couldn't be simpler. This Sweet Potato and Sausage Hash makes a great breakfast or brunch, and can be topped with some eggs or eaten on its own. And all it takes is six ingredients to get there.

The dish starts with some onions and garlic sautéed in butter. These are then combined with cooked Italian sausage and cubed sweet potatoes. Everything is roasted together in a cast-iron skillet, showing how you can make this recipe with minimal effort and maximum tastiness.

There are never enough ways to use up those extra potatoes! This time, your floury potatoes like Yukon Golds or Russets take the lead with an herby potato galette. This particular recipe is a crustless galette, so there's no dough necessary, and you only need a handful of ingredients to make it.

To make the galette, shred the potatoes, add them to a hot skillet with lots of olive oil and sage, then press them down to help form a natural crust. Cook the potatoes for another 10 minutes as butter is added to the pan, then flip the whole thing and cook it on the other side. The result is a crispy potato pancake that's golden on the outside, soft on the inside, and delicious all the way around.

It's the ultimate Thanksgiving grilled cheese, so you don't want to pass this one up. You can make use of several leftover ingredients for this sandwich, both savory and sweet, such as extra apples and leftover ham.

Apple butter is spread across two slices of sourdough bread, and then layered with Brie, diced ham, and diced apples before the sandwich is toasted in butter. This simply isn't your average grilled cheese sandwich; you also get bonus points if you can pair it with some butternut squash soup.

Recipe: Sweet and Savory Brie and Apple Butter Grilled Cheese

#9680. The State With The Most Wendy's Locations Isn't New York, California, Or Texas

Wendy's is a beloved chain of fast food restaurants whose square-shaped burger patties are instantly recognizable to many American diners. Founded in 1969 in Columbus, Ohio, the brand is an institution where it was born — yet the Midwestern state doesn't actually have the most locations. Neither do populous hubs like California or New York. Rather, you need to look southeast to the land of orange groves. With 464 restaurants as of November 2026, Florida has more Wendy's locations than any other state in the country.

The Sunshine State accounts for roughly 8% of the total number of locations this fast food giant has in the United States, compared to Texas, which has slightly fewer locations at 419. However, if you take population differences into account, there are more restaurants per capita in Florida than in the Lone Star State. This means that Florida residents are more likely to find a Wendy's nearby. Not everything seems to be bigger in Texas, after all, at least when it comes to this fast food chain.

Additionally, two Florida cities — Miami and Orlando — are in the top five U.S. cities with the most Wendy's locations (per ScrapeHero). So, whether you're enjoying the nightlife of South Beach or visiting Disney World, you won't be too far from a Jr. Bacon Cheeseburger. Despite Florida's distinction of having the most locations, however, it doesn't have the largest Wendy's in the world. That honor goes to Tbilisi, the capital of Georgia, a country in the Caucasus region.

The idea of people vacationing in, moving to, or spending part of the year in Florida is an old trope, and there's a good reason for it. Many Americans see the state as a respite from the cold, and the Sunshine State actually has a long history of being a destination for migrants moving down from northern states, dating back to as early as the 1800s.

Interestingly, people from Ohio comprise a large portion of these migrants — in fact, according to USAFacts, more Ohioans moved to Florida than to any other state in 2024. Just like immigrants from other countries, American transplants bring their own cultures that can influence the local culinary scene, and maybe that's why there are so many Wendy's locations in the Sunshine State.

Considering how the brand was founded in the Buckeye State, perhaps the many transplants brought their taste for the chain's iconic baked potatoes, chili, and square burgers with them. After all, Ohio has the third-largest number of Wendy's restaurants and has more locations per capita than Florida. It might seem like mere coincidence until you take into account the fact that Florida is also home to another Buckeye institution, Skyline Chili, and it's the only state outside the Midwest where the chain is present.

#9679. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.

#9675. Crostata Di Mele (Italian Apple Pie) Recipe

While working as a young pastry chef in an Italian trattoria, I had the great fortune of spending 3 weeks eating my way through Italy in an attempt to discover the most unique and tempting desserts each region had to offer. Although I tasted complex and ethereal cakes, pastries, and frozen delights, I kept coming back to the simple fruit crostatas: buttery crusts molded into tart pans or baked free-form in rustic rounds, topped with glistening fruits and cakey or custardy fillings. These desserts tasted like perfection in their simplicity and purity of flavors.

My recipe for crostata di Mele (Italian apple pie) is a bakery-worthy homage to those delightful desserts, and it became a seasonal fixture on my pastry menu. A traditional pasta frolla (Italian short dough) crust is filled with a lemon and vanilla-scented creme patissiere (pastry cream custard) and topped with tart, crisp apples and crunchy turbinado sugar. The warm crostata is given a finishing glaze of melted apricot preserves, then chilled for serving.

Learning how to make the dough and filling for this crostata will give you a solid foundation for making other Italian pastries. The dough is easy to work with, and the pastry cream is a versatile filling for other treats, such as profiteroles, layer cakes, or napoleons.

There are 3 main components in the crostata di mele: the crust, the custard filling, and the toppings. For the crust, you will need all-purpose flour, granulated sugar, sea salt, cold unsalted butter, a large egg plus 1 yolk, vanilla extract, and the zest of a large lemon. The difference between this crostata dough and regular apple pie dough is the addition of eggs, which makes the dough slightly less flaky but more pliable for rolling and shaping. For the pastry cream, you will need whole milk, a vanilla bean, more lemon zest, 4 yolks, granulated sugar, and cornstarch. You will split the vanilla bean lengthwise to release the tiny black seeds into the milk, and the cornstarch acts as a thickening agent. To top the crostata, I like using apples that are crisp and tart, but that also have a balance of sweetness. Honeycrisp, Pink Lady, and Granny Smith are perfect apple varieties for this recipe. You will toss your apple slices with fresh lemon juice to prevent browning before baking, and use some melted butter to secure a crunchy sprinkling of turbinado sugar. To give your baked crostata a shiny finish, you will need apricot preserves to melt down and strain.

Combine the flour, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer bowl.

Add the butter a few pieces at a time and mix until pea-sized clumps form.

Add the egg, yolk, lemon zest, and vanilla, and mix until a dough forms.

Shape the dough into a disk, wrap in plastic, and refrigerate it for at least 30 minutes.

While the dough is chilling, heat the milk, vanilla bean, and lemon zest strips in a medium saucepan until it barely starts to simmer.

Remove the pan from the heat, cover, and steep for 10 minutes.

Place a medium glass bowl on a damp kitchen towel or mat to prevent slipping.

Add the egg yolks, sugar, and cornstarch and whisk until thick and pale yellow.

Remove the vanilla bean and zest strips with a slotted spoon, then discard.

Gradually add the warm milk to the egg mixture, whisking constantly.

Transfer the mixture back to the saucepan and cook over low heat, stirring frequently until it comes to a boil. Turn the heat to low and whisk constantly for 1 minute.

Remove the pan from the heat, then scrape the filling into a heat-proof bowl and press a piece of plastic wrap to the surface. Chill for at least 2 hours.

In a large bowl, toss the apple slices with the lemon juice.

Roll out the chilled dough to a 12-inch circle on a floured surface.

Roll out the chilled dough to a 12-inch circle on a floured surface.

Press the dough into the pan and trim the excess flush with the edge of the pan.

Spread the cooled pastry cream evenly over the bottom of the pastry shell.

Arrange the slices in concentric overlapping circles over the pastry cream, starting from the outer edge and working inward.

Brush the apples with the melted butter and sprinkle on the turbinado sugar.

Bake the crostata di mele for about 50 minutes until the crust is golden brown and the apples are tender.

While the crostata is baking, heat the apricot jam with 1 tablespoon of water in a small saucepan until warm and liquid.

Strain the jam if any large pieces of fruit remain.

Remove the crostata from the oven and immediately brush on the apricot glaze.

Cool the crostata completely in the pan on a rack before removing from the pan.

Slice the crostata and serve at room temperature or chilled.

Our bakery-worthy crostata di Mele (Italian apple pie) is filled with a lemon and vanilla-scented creme patissiere and topped with tart, crisp apples.

The crostata is one of the most continuously made dessert forms found in Italian baking, dating back to the 1400s. Not only is the crostata found in pastry shops and on restaurant menus, but it is also the one dessert that many people make at home with whatever ingredients are on hand. This kind of humble tart was likely consumed at breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

The crostata di mele probably originated in northern Italy, where apples are grown in abundance. In order to highlight the fresh flavor of the apples, crostata de mele is spiced with a light hand. Subtle cinnamon and a hint of nutmeg might be used, along with the zest of a lemon, as in this recipe. With only a few simple ingredients, the recipe is also dependent on using a light hand in preparation. The dough should be minimally handled to prevent a tough or shrunken crust. The pastry cream must be carefully tempered to prevent lumps from forming. And nothing should get in the way of the apples being the star.

Even though there may seem to be a lot of steps to this recipe, there are lots of ways to do advance prep to save time. First, your crostata dough can be mixed, shaped into a disk, wrapped, and chilled for several days in the refrigerator. You can also freeze this dough for up to 3 months. Once you are ready to roll out the dough, allow it to come to cool to room temperature before you shape it. You can also roll out and fill your tart pan, then wrap the unbaked shell and refrigerate or freeze until it is time to fill and bake.

The pastry cream should only be made 1 or 2 days in advance, and this custardy filling should not be frozen unless it is layered into a dessert (too much separation will occur). Wait until just before baking to spread the pastry cream into your tart shell so that the dough will not become soggy.

From experience, I know that this crostata di mele will stay fresh, tasty, and sliceable for almost a week under refrigeration. That said, it is crucial to always keep the crostata chilled to prevent bacterial growth in the custard layer. Typically, 3-5 days is the best range for serving this dessert.
